item.title: SeverVault: Infostealer Logs Sold as AI Victim Profiles
item.description:
SeverVault, a stealer log shop advertised on DarkForums on November 14, 2026, attaches an AI-written profile to each log naming the likely employer and access. Listings tie $9 to $10 logs to government, defense and bank households.
- What was advertised: The seller claims tens of millions of logs, more than a billion parsed accounts, a $0.25 entry price and free registration, all of it the seller's own claim and unverified. Operators are unknown, and the thread came from a newly registered account with a single post. Vidar and Rhadamanthys appear in the listings seen so far.
- What a listing contains: The usual stealer metadata (stealer family, OS and build, country, state, city, ISP, counts of links, saved passwords and cookies) now sits under an AI headline, a short narrative, a score out of 100 and tags. Tags name organization domains, SSO providers such as Okta and Auth0, GitHub, Jira, Workday, and wallets such as Exodus, MetaMask and Trust Wallet. Scores seen ran from 54 to 100, with no explanation of the method.
- Who is being profiled: One listing describes a Los Angeles County official's workstation with live sessions on SSA, USCIS and EDD portals plus a private RDP key. Others cover a Virginia government official, a DC government employee's family computer, and a Maryland machine titled "The Defense Contractor and Student Household Dump" with corporate SSO and Citrix access. "The Bank Employee Family's Shared Workstation" is a Texas Windows 11 Vidar log, $9, scored 100/100, with Citrix and SSO traces, saved credentials for major US 🇺🇸 banks, live Steam and Discord tokens and eight Google OAuth refresh tokens.
- Why it matters: Most of these are household or shared machines outside corporate endpoint controls, yet they carry work sessions. The profiles may be wrong or blend several users, but narrowing millions of logs to bank staff, contractors and government employees is enough to turn opportunistic theft into targeted initial access. Session cookies and OAuth refresh tokens are the most immediate risk, since a still-valid session can be replayed without a new MFA prompt.
- Infrastructure from the advertisement: clearnet domains sever[.]to, sever[.]ws, sever[.]cx and sever[.]st, plus four onion mirrors.
DFIR takeaway: treat any employee exposure in a profiled log as an endpoint compromise, not just a credential reset. Map every account, app and token the log touches, including remote access, SaaS and API platforms. Clean or rebuild the device before issuing new credentials, then reset passwords and revoke active sessions, refresh tokens and API keys in the same step. Hunt authentication and audit logs for sign-ins, session reuse or API activity since the infection date. Upstream, require device compliance checks for Citrix, VPN and SaaS sign-ins and shorten session lifetimes so a stolen cookie ages out fast. The four clearnet domains and the onion addresses are listed in the report for blocking and monitoring.

item.title: Optimizely hack infected CNN, Fox News, BBC, Salesforce sites with malware
item.description:
A flaw in Optimizely's Experimentation signup flow let an attacker inject JavaScript into customer projects, so CNN, BBC, Salesforce and others served a card skimmer, crypto clipper and iOS exploit kits.
This is a classic third-party script supply chain compromise. Victim sites were never breached directly. Their trusted Optimizely JavaScript files were modified upstream, so the malicious code ran in visitors' browsers with the full privileges of the first-party page. Optimizely says the attacker abused the signup flow to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects, and the company has since blocked the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.
- Scope: researcher Scott Helme analyzed 1,611 Optimizely scripts and found 188 infected files belonging to 178 organizations. BleepingComputer confirmed via urlscan[.]io that the payload loaded, or tried to load, on Zoom, GitLab, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, KLM, Smartsheet, Stamps[.]com, Fox News, Air France 🇫🇷, HSBC Insurance, Bitly, UNICEF USA 🇺🇸 and others. Salesforce is disabling Optimizely scripts across preview and production instances while it investigates.
- Injection method: the modified files pull a second stage from hxxps://1688360[.]cc/track.js. Some reference the URL directly, others hide it as Base64 and decode it with JavaScript's atob(). Helme also found a variant that runs an embedded copy of the malicious code if the remote script is blocked, so blocking the domain alone may not neutralize every sample.
- Payload capabilities: track.js swaps cryptocurrency wallet addresses on the page for attacker-controlled ones, scrapes card numbers, expiry dates and security codes and sends them to hxxps://1688360[.]cc/card.php, and collects cookies, page URLs and screenshots. It also loads secondary JavaScript that Helme identified as the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits, which target different iOS versions.
- Impact and timeline: the earliest observed injection was in the early morning of November 16. It is still unclear how long the vulnerability existed or how many visitors were exposed. Wallets in the script had received about $7,000 as of November 16, but some were active before the attack, so true theft is hard to measure. Only one of the 188 files still held malicious code as of 21:52 UTC on November 16. Optimizely also ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts and blocked code delivery in Cloudflare.
Takeaway for responders: if your sites load Optimizely, treat November 16 onward as the exposure window, as one file was still infected late that day. These requests come from visitors' browsers, not your servers, so search web proxy and DNS logs for 1688360[.]cc, especially track.js and card.php, to find exposed users. Diff your cached or archived Optimizely snippets against known-good copies, and grep for atob() and Base64 blobs that decode to that URL. Preserve the infected copies before they are overwritten, since the vendor cleanup is removing evidence. Review Optimizely account activity, sessions and tokens for your project, and check any Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity coverage. The report lists the full wallet address table for tracing clipper transfers. Affected users should check crypto transfers made on November 16, watch card accounts, and update iOS and iPadOS.

item.title: Optimizely supply chain attack infects major brands' sites with malware
item.description:
A suspected Optimizely supply chain attack injected malicious JavaScript into 188 CDN-hosted files across 178 organizations, hitting Zoom, CNN, BBC and others with crypto hijacking, card skimming and iOS exploit kits.
Security researcher Scott Helme reported the campaign after analyzing 1,611 scripts used by the platform. Optimizely is an experimentation and personalization platform whose JavaScript runs inside customers' pages, so a change to a customer project reaches every visitor of that site. BleepingComputer confirmed the malicious script loaded, or tried to load, on sites including Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, Smartsheet, Stamps[.]com, Fox News, Air France 🇫🇷, HSBC Insurance and Bitly, using urlscan[.]io scans.
- Attack chain: attackers inserted code into Optimizely customer projects, so JavaScript hosted on Optimizely's CDN pulled in a second-stage script from hxxps://1688360[.]cc/track.js. Some files reference the URL directly. Others hide it with Base64 and JavaScript's atob() function. Helme also found a variant that runs an embedded copy of the payload if the remote script is blocked, so blocking the domain alone may not stop it. Helme traced the earliest hijacking to early morning on November 16.
- What track.js does: it watches pages for cryptocurrency wallet addresses and swaps in attacker-controlled ones. It searches for card numbers, expiration dates and security codes entered on pages and tries to send them to hxxps://1688360[.]cc/card.php. It can also collect browser cookies, page URLs and screenshots for transmission to the attackers.
- iOS exploitation: the script loads secondary JavaScript aimed at iPhones and iPads. Helme identified these payloads as the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits, each targeting different iOS versions. Visitors on unpatched iOS devices face more than data theft.
- Impact: the clipboard-hijacking component worked. Wallets embedded in track.js received roughly $7,000 on November 16, mostly Bitcoin (about $5,380 across 7 transactions), plus Litecoin, TRON/USDT, Ethereum and BNB Smart Chain USDT. The full wallet list is in BleepingComputer's report. Helme reported cleanup had left only one of the 188 files still malicious as of 21:52 UTC on November 16.
- Open questions: it is unknown how the attackers got access to so many customer projects. The report does not say whether Optimizely's infrastructure was compromised, credentials were stolen, or another method was used. BleepingComputer has asked Optimizely for comment. Attribution is not given.
Takeaway: if your pages load Optimizely, recover archived or cached copies of the Optimizely JavaScript your site served on November 16; most infected files were cleaned that day, so a fresh fetch may look clean. Search them for 1688360[.]cc, atob() calls that decode URLs, and embedded fallback payloads. Look for visitor-browser requests to track.js and card.php in CSP reports or client-side telemetry, and treat anyone who entered card data on affected pages in that window as exposed. Review who and what could modify your Optimizely projects, since initial access is still unexplained. urlscan[.]io records of your pages can show whether the script loaded. The wallet addresses are in the report.

item.title: ARTEX and Storm-0940: How an AI Attack Framework Became a Growing Threat to Cloud Tenants
item.description:
Microsoft assesses China-aligned Storm-0940 used the ARTEX AI attack framework to compromise a vendor's M365 apps, then tried sign-ins against 2,250+ tenants with valid credentials.
ARTEX is an open-source pen-testing framework that runs AI agents with little human direction. It went from GitHub project to attacker staple in about three months, and none of the documented cloud campaigns used a Microsoft vulnerability.
- Storm-0940 chain, per Microsoft's Oct 21 report: a password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between Oct 10 and 14 produced hundreds of thousands of failed attempts, peaking at thousands per minute on Oct 11. The actor then took over the vendor's app identities, authenticated as service principals, ran Microsoft Graph recon, added credentials to existing OAuth apps, and read secrets across multiple Key Vaults. In one tenant a management app assigned itself Global Administrator. Google tracks overlapping activity as UNC7228 against US 🇺🇸 and European enterprise software, industrial automation, semiconductor and telecom targets. Wiz says the actor has since moved on to other IT and software vendors, focusing on Okta, Entra and M365 integrations.
- Why it is hard to catch: Microsoft saw one agent go from searching GitHub to exfiltrating from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. Google saw bursts of 2 to 25 seconds, including 27 events in 23 seconds. Agents self-correct: a failed Key Vault batch with the wrong API version was retried correctly about 28 seconds later. They also rotate fingerprints once blocked, and Wiz saw 15+ user-agent strings. Service principals do not sign in interactively and face no MFA prompts, so user-focused controls miss them.
- Beyond cloud: Storm-3358 used ARTEX against internet-facing systems, exploiting anonymous file upload and SSRF flaws. Agents then pulled down WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2 with netcat and curl. Microsoft says agents repeatedly focused on credentials that give access to AI services. Exposed secrets feed much of this: Apiiro found 2,539 secrets across 1,994 public GitHub repos in AI coding agent settings files.
- Indicators from Microsoft, Google and Wiz, all short-lived: Storm-0940 IPs 144.172.64[.]99, 144.172.64[.]60, 144.172.64[.]128, 104.194.150[.]21 and 167.88.172[.]97. Storm-3358 servers include 91.92.240[.]238 and 85.11.168[.]45, with C2 at 85.11.167[.]52. Host artifacts: files named artex-probe-* with roughly incrementing five-digit numbers, accounts with ArtexProbe in the name and plaintext passwords, short-lived JSP webshells like cl1217.jsp and f1219a.jsp (one written via MySQL general log poisoning), and outbound traffic to rotating webhook[.]site URLs (491 in one Google-observed intrusion).
Takeaway: hunt service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs, not just user sign-ins. Look for one source authenticating as multiple service principals, one app requesting tokens for several Azure services in minutes, a failed request corrected within a minute, and bursts of dozens of events in seconds. In every tenant, check for credentials newly added to OAuth apps and any app assigning itself Global Administrator. Inventory third-party multi-tenant apps, and review what each consented app could reach. A successful app sign-in does not prove data access, but it sets your scoping. More IPs (incl. WISP C2 nodes) and the client strings are in Todyl's write-up; Microsoft calls its own list sample indicators. Treat them as a starting point, since agents rotate infrastructure once blocked.

item.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
item.description:
Microsoft saw a high-volume phishing wave on November 13, 2026 using fake Microsoft 365 outage notices to push a "RESTORE MESSAGES" link. Likely credential phishing, but credential capture was not confirmed.
- The lure: emails posed as Microsoft 365 service-health notices. Subjects start with "Outage" plus a random token. Display names pair a three-character org-style prefix with "Outage Notification" or "Service Health". One body cited an Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed four messages were held, and set a 24-hour deletion deadline. The body also carried a fake hidden email conversation, which looks like a filter-evasion attempt.
- Infrastructure: sender domains are moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com, with bounce subdomains em4493.moments-notice[.]com and em.newbooker[.]com. Links went through recipient-specific click-tracking hosts, including the campaign's url.newbooker[.]com and shared SendGrid hosts such as u113727626.ct.sendgrid[.]net. They landed on reallifeaccounting[.]com, sometimes with the path /themelist0.html. Some messages pointed to outagefixed[.]sbs or outagerestored[.]sbs. A tracking-pixel host sits at 162.120.17[.]69:8080.
- What was not seen: no QR codes, no attachments beyond EML, and no executable, archive or document payloads. Microsoft did not have the final page source, credential fields or submission telemetry, so there is no attribution to a named actor or malware family. The report maps only T1566.002 (spearphishing link), T1036 (masquerading) and T1204.001 (malicious link).
- Scope and risk: the campaign targeted organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. If a user did enter credentials, the report flags account compromise, mailbox access, BEC, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft says protected environments blocked and quarantined the messages and that it observed no indicators of compromise from the attack.
Takeaway: scope this as a click-and-credential question, not a malware one. Search mail telemetry for the sender domains, the Outage subject pattern, display-name patterns and the tracking hosts, then pivot to click telemetry, proxy and endpoint logs to see who reached the destination. For anyone who may have submitted credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and verify MFA registrations. Then review sign-ins, new devices, OAuth consent, inbox and forwarding rules, and delegate permissions. Do not block shared email-delivery domains wholesale; combine sender, content, URL and behavior signals. The report includes KQL hunting queries, and its IOC table also lists two more subject patterns ("Strengthen - Security", "Restore - 4 messages").

Takeaway: scope this as a click-and-credential question, not a malware one. Search mail telemetry for the sender domains, the Outage subject pattern, display-name patterns and the tracking hosts, then pivot to click telemetry, proxy and endpoint logs to see who reached the destination. For anyone who may have submitted credentials, reset the password, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, and verify MFA registrations. Then review sign-ins, new devices, OAuth consent, inbox and forwarding rules, and delegate permissions. Do not block shared email-delivery domains wholesale; combine sender, content, URL and behavior signals. The report includes KQL hunting queries, and its IOC table also lists two more subject patterns ("Strengthen - Security", "Restore - 4 messages").

item.title: Crypto hardware wallet users under attack
item.description:
A campaign aimed at crypto and hardware wallet users uses fake wallet software and tax-file lures to get victims to run a BAT file that installs ConnectWise ScreenConnect. Once it is in, the attacker has remote control, command execution, and access to whatever is on the box.
- Lures are branded to the victim's wallet or service. Observed names include Coldcard v1.5.3Q-q1-coldcard (.zip and .bat, coldcard[.]pro), Ledger-wallet-Transition-Transcript (.zip and .bat, ledger-wallet[.]net and ledgeradvisorinfo[.]app), and Pera_Algorand_Wallet_v2.1.2.35 (.zip and .bat, peraalgowallet[.]app). Tax-themed lures cover Revolut (revolut-taxfile[.]zip and .bat) and Xaman (xamantaxfile[.]zip). The Pera and Revolut BAT files share the same SHA-256 in the report's table: f7f646ce988f9af34075792805b786aea16a53d67c5cda5cbbe484f37b2fa1af.
- The chain is user-driven. The victim downloads the ZIP and runs the BAT inside. Batch files (T1059.003) execute commands and launch later stages, and PowerShell (T1059.001) is used to start processes, bypass execution policy, and run commands in a hidden window. The ScreenConnect installer (screenconnect.msi or screenconnect.exe) is then staged on the host (T1105). The report ties both to fjksdjfdtitive[.]net as the remote-access server. The MSI SHA-256 is b3418cfb2a5b36682429b10443cd5333d19346fee83e8b85d7f6947b4ad3fa4a.
- Persistence and C2 are legitimate-tool abuse. ScreenConnect is installed as a Windows service (T1543.003) and deployed as remote desktop software (T1219.002). The client calls back to fjksdjfdtitive[.]net on TCP 8041 (T1571). The report also gives IP 191.96.101[.]224 and the connection parameters h= (remote host), s= (session identifier), e=Access, and y=Guest. The attacker logs in through a ScreenConnect login page on that domain to control the device.
- Host artifacts are easy to check. Look in Installed Apps or Programs and Features for ScreenConnect Client (abb21f5ccc9bd236; the ID suffix can differ per installation). The install directory is C:\Program Files (x86)\ScreenConnect Client (abb21f5ccc9bd236)\ and holds ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe, ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe, and ScreenConnect.WindowsBackstageShell.exe. Check services.msc for a ScreenConnect Client service. Also check %TEMP% for leftover .bat files and for folders starting with sc_installer_, which may remain if the install itself is gone.
- Impact is full remote access. The attacker can run commands and steal data, so locally stored wallet data, email, password manager, and exchange credentials should all be treated as exposed.
Takeaway: unless your organization or the user actually runs ScreenConnect, treat any presence as compromise. Hunt for ScreenConnect client installs, services, and sc_installer_ folders on endpoints. Search proxy, DNS, and firewall logs for fjksdjfdtitive[.]net and 191.96.101[.]224, and for outbound TCP 8041. Look at downloaded ZIPs and BAT files in user download paths and %TEMP% as the likely entry point.
If you find it: isolate the host, stop and disable the service before removing files, and reinstall Windows, as the report recommends. Reset email, password manager, and exchange credentials from a separate clean device. Revoke sessions, API keys, and suspicious token approvals. If a recovery phrase or private key may have been exposed, treat the wallet as compromised and move funds to a new wallet generated on a clean device.
The report lists IOCs in its tables, with the complete set on a LevelBlue (AlienVault) OTX pulse.

item.title: QUIC and Covert: Novel HTTP/3-Powered RATs Target Southeast Asian Governments
item.description:
TGR-STA-0049 (aka REF7707, Earth Alux, Ink Dragon) has hit Southeast Asian government networks since at least July 2025 with two new custom RATs, PerfectPioneer and KUKURAT. Both use HTTP/3 (QUIC over UDP) for C2, which may slip past TCP-centric inspection.
- Initial access: Exchange and web server exploitation is the primary vector, dropping web shells including ASPXSpy, Godzilla, Bysunue.aspx and Suo5. The report names no CVE. Phishing is secondary: executables with PDF icons served from lookalike government domains, including a decoy PDF impersonating a Myanmar 🇲🇲 Union Election Commission document. The RAT also ships via DLL side-loading (a tampered legitimate binary carrying XOR-encrypted shellcode) and decoy installers, one of which ran a real GlobalProtect installer while the agent executed in the background.
- PerfectPioneer RAT (Go, six variants): HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback. C2 paths are /agent/register, /agent/heartbeat, /agent/tasks and /agent/result. Persistence is an HKCU Run key plus a Startup folder .lnk. A cleanup routine deletes its own temp files. The Pioneer and rat_http3_cc variants carry isDangerousCommand, a blocklist that stops operators from running noisy or destructive commands such as disk wipes, reg delete, bcdedit, firewall flushes and encoded PowerShell. rat_http3_cc also runs a local monitoring HTTP server on port 56793.
- KUKURAT (C++, seen since March 2026, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 variants): a modular framework that loads capability DLLs from the C2 into memory, so the core binary has little to scan. Modules cover screenshots, keylogging, scanning, SOCKS tunneling, PsExec lateral movement, SMB brute-forcing and BOF execution. Heartbeats go to a hashed path, /c8a4e192. Its heuristic camouflage, toggled by set_obfuscation, generates decoy HTTP requests, registry activity and temp file churn. The registry noise writes, reads and deletes HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, then enumerates HKCU\Software\Google\Update\ClientState. The extra PsExecService.exe module registers a service named PsExec with the named pipe \\.\pipe\PSEXEC, and uninstalls itself after five minutes of inactivity. The watchdog uses the pipe WINDOW_SEC_WATCHDOG and was seen in C:\ProgramData\Cyvera\Ransomware\, a path mimicking a security product.
- Domain and credential tradecraft: after compromising a Domain Controller, the actor planted malicious log-on scripts that download KUKURAT whenever a user authenticates. Credential theft used LSASS dumping via rundll32 and comsvcs.dll, calling the ordinal #+000024 instead of MiniDump by name and writing to \Windows\Temp\MxA.tar. The actor also used DCSync, Mimikatz, ProcDump, SharpDPAPI and SAM/SYSTEM hive dumps.
- Mail and exfiltration: from the Exchange foothold, PowerShell checked Get-ManagementRoleAssignment -Role:ApplicationImpersonation. When that failed, the actor looped Get-Mailbox through Add-MailboxPermission to grant a compromised account FullAccess on every mailbox. Targeted data was .pdf, .docx, .xlsx and .png files focused on international relations and internal political affairs.
Takeaway: hunt for outbound UDP 443 from servers and DCs that have no business speaking QUIC, or block it to force fallback to inspectable TCP. Review SYSVOL and GPO log-on script changes, and check service-install records for a service named PsExec (it self-removes) and the \\.\pipe\PSEXEC pipe. Search for rundll32 calling comsvcs.dll with #+000024, and for MxA.tar in \Windows\Temp. In Exchange logs, look for Add-MailboxPermission FullAccess loops and the ApplicationImpersonation role. KUKURAT C2 domains include www.cloudflacecdn[.]com, www.police[.]gr[.]com and www.investigationj6[.]com. The report separately lists IPs 27.254.164[.]212 and 27.254.164[.]209, not tied to KUKURAT C2. File hashes, web shell hashes and full domain lists are in the report's IOC section, with command lists in its appendices.

item.title: CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts
item.description:
CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9) in ScreenConnect is exploited in the wild, listed in CISA KEV since Sept 11. A guest can push a file to an MSP technician's host client and have it run with no prompt, and Huntress saw a full compromise in 9 seconds.
- The flaw: ConnectWise disclosed it Sept 8. In Support and Access sessions, a guest can trigger file-transfer actions that the technician's host client processes without authorization or confirmation, including running the file with elevated rights. The vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine, so patching the server alone does not fix it. The fixed version is 26.6.5 for host clients and Access agents. The interim mitigation is removing the TransferFiles permission. Many technicians were still on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after the fix.
- 9-second chain (Nov 12, UTC): the host client ran a guest-pushed update_224ac089.bat. The script relaunched hidden via PowerShell and WScript[.]Shell, decoded a Base64 Telegram bot token to report the victim, and ran recon (reg query, net session). It then used curl to pull hxxps://masterdarky[.]com/WindowsUpdate.msi to %TEMP%\wupdate_224ac089.msi. msiexec /a unpacked it as an administrative image to %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_224ac089, which leaves no install record. It set seclogon to auto start, launched the payload with runas /trustlevel:0x20000, and started WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe, a rebranded ScreenConnect client talking to the relay on port 8041. ATT&CK: T1203, T1218.007, T1543.003, T1134.002.
- The spray: across 42 MSP servers between Oct 20 and Nov 16, attacker guests made 688,000 run-file requests for update.bat or update_<8hex>.bat from 29 IPs, waiting for a technician to join. The exact file update_224ac089.bat hit five servers within 2 seconds of each other, 43 minutes before the compromise. Spray sessions had blank or default-looking names, and 27 across 17 servers carried Company property (CustomProperty1) set to crypto client.
- Targeted activity: guest 91.224.92[.]167, which looked hand-operated, pushed marker.txt as a canary 2 seconds after the technician joined, and it opened in Notepad++ about 3 seconds after the push. In October, attackers joined real customer support sessions as extra guests and requested a traversal path to ../../../AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/STARTM~1/Programs/Startup/Sync.bat from 193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66, aiming for logon persistence (T1547.001). The Mac client failed on the Windows path. Run-Lateral.bat and svc_payload.cmd were also pushed, and some pushes missed by seconds.
- Hunt on the server: work on a copy of App_Data\Session.db and look for RanFiles (EventType 85) or SentFiles (86) from a guest connection (ProcessType = 2). Then check whether a Host connection (ProcessType = 1) was open at that moment. That overlap is the exposure. Flag any path containing ../ and high-volume requests from one guest session.
- Hunt on workstations: ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or notepad from Documents\*\Temp\ with RunFile in the parent arguments. Also look for unexpected files in the Startup folder (especially Sync.bat), wclient_<8hex> folders, wupdate_<8hex>.msi, and any ScreenConnect client pointing at a relay you do not own.
Takeaway: Patch every technician client to 26.6.5 or later, then run the Session.db overlap check to see who was connected while a guest pushed files. If a workstation hits, isolate it, remove the wclient and wupdate artifacts, reset seclogon, and rotate every credential reachable from it (RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, vault, customer admin). Huntress's report has the IOC table (relay domain, hash, sprayer and operator IPs, file names) and the full ATT&CK mapping.

item.title: Poisoned Scripts on BBC, Zoom and Other Major Websites Linked to iPhone Exploit Loaders
item.description:
Poisoned third-party JavaScript on BBC, Zoom, GitLab and HSBC UAE 🇦🇪 swaps crypto addresses, skims cards, and routes iPhones to Coruna and DarkSword exploit-kit infrastructure.
- Delivery: the report confirms malicious code in responses served by four providers' own endpoints: Optimizely projectJS, Kissmetrics (a 213-byte shared i.js loader), StorifyMe widgets and a 561-byte minute-ly loader. Kirk from Ohey supplied 15 archived website captures covering 16 vendor responses, and Hudson Rock matched the hashes. Together the evidence names 21 web properties, including CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, Mutual of Omaha, FAZ and the Sydney Morning Herald. Initial access to each provider is unknown, and the report does not show the sites' own backends were compromised.
- Browser payload: the Optimizely injections load 1688360[.]cc/track.js (29,882 bytes, SHA-256 f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40). It swaps wallet addresses for EVM, Bitcoin, TRON, TON, Solana, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin. It hooks forms, fetch and XHR for Luhn-valid card data, sent to 1688360[.]cc/card.php with fields n, e, c and u. A conditional hit.php POST carries up to 8,000 characters of readable cookies plus an html2canvas JPEG. HttpOnly cookies stay out of reach. No victim counts or successful thefts are established.
- Mobile branch: Kissmetrics, StorifyMe, minute-ly and an earlier BBC response load webshell[.]lol/get.js with channel marker 02111110. It leads to boot.js routers on 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu and eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, with A8 entries tied to Coruna and D11 labelled DarkSword. The C10 route for iOS 26 is configured but untested. urlscan captures with iOS user-agent strings got HTTP 200 on entry stages, but urlscan runs headless Chrome. This is delivery evidence only: no successful iPhone exploitation and no zero-day is shown.
- Containment trap: the BBC and HSBC UAE 🇦🇪 scripts embed the full 24,392-byte payload in Base64 (SHA-256 c2a34c579e4c2e8802752c93b3a9cca0230610f3e4dd6688f4272459c7c7c162). It runs if the remote fetch errors or exceeds 2.5 seconds, so blocking 1688360[.]cc does not stop local address substitution. The minute-ly loader removes its own script elements after three seconds, so DOM-only inspection can be incomplete. Later clean copies of some assets do not invalidate the earlier archive hashes.
Takeaway: before restoring anything, preserve the actual response bytes, headers, hashes, timestamps and project revisions. Then review project changes, publication history, account activity, API credentials and integrations with each affected provider. Hunt card.php and hit.php POSTs, boot and entry-stage requests, and /api/gs_state or /api/pe_ok calls as separate events, since pe_ok alone does not prove privilege escalation. Combine markers such as ds_vk, __DAILI_CFG, chainFrame and window._k7 with origin and path, never alone. Seek device-level forensics if iPhone exposure is suspected. IOCs, hashes and wallet destinations are in Hudson Rock's report. Handle evidence carefully, since the card-deduplication keys can contain card details.

This is delivery evidence only: no successful iPhone exploitation and no zero-day is shown.

- Containment trap: the BBC and HSBC UAE 🇦🇪 scripts embed the full 24,392-byte payload in Base64 (SHA-256 c2a34c579e4c2e8802752c93b3a9cca0230610f3e4dd6688f4272459c7c7c162). It runs if the remote fetch errors or exceeds 2.5 seconds, so blocking 1688360[.]cc does not stop local address substitution. The minute-ly loader removes its own script elements after three seconds, so DOM-only inspection can be incomplete. Later clean copies of some assets do not invalidate the earlier archive hashes.

Takeaway: before restoring anything, preserve the actual response bytes, headers, hashes, timestamps and project revisions. Then review project changes, publication history, account activity, API credentials and integrations with each affected provider. Hunt card.php and hit.php POSTs, boot and entry-stage requests, and /api/gs_state or /api/pe_ok calls as separate events, since pe_ok alone does not prove privilege escalation. Combine markers such as ds_vk, __DAILI_CFG, chainFrame and window._k7 with origin and path, never alone. Seek device-level forensics if iPhone exposure is suspected. IOCs, hashes and wallet destinations are in Hudson Rock's report. Handle evidence carefully, since the card-deduplication keys can contain card details.

item.title: Detections Digest #20261116
item.description:
Between Nov 9 and Nov 16, 2026, contributors to five monitored GitHub repos added 28 rules and updated 27. The week's themes are BITS upload abuse, React Server Components exploitation, DLL search order hijacking, and monitoring of enterprise AI agent MCP servers.
- BITS gets its other half. Splunk security_content added Windows BITS Upload Activity, which flags bitsadmin.exe with /create or /transfer plus /upload or /upload-reply, and PowerShell Start-BitsTransfer with Upload or UploadReply transfer types. That covers data staging and exfil through the Background Intelligent Transfer Service. The existing BITSAdmin Download File and PowerShell Start-BitsTransfer rules were tuned toward direct IP connections, public hosting services, sensitive staging paths, and chained process execution (Ingress Tool Transfer, T1105). BITS Job Persistence now extracts /SetNotifyCmdLine arguments and drops empty ones, so the callback command is the thing you read.
- Two new Defender queries from benscha/KQLAdvancedHunting. Reverse Shell Spawned from Vulnerable React Server Components flags Node.js processes running reverse shell or download-cradle syntax in command interpreters, then matches them to outbound public connections within five minutes. It targets react-server-dom-* exposure. DLL Hijacking via Print Spooler, WBEM and WER Paths correlates low or medium integrity modification of Printconfig.dll, tzres.dll, or phoneinfo.dll with a later image load by SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, or NETWORK SERVICE within 30 minutes, checking file path and SHA1 match. The digest says nothing about observed exploitation in either case. These are hunting logic, not incident reports.
- AI agent visibility is arriving as detection content. Three Sentinel queries use the AgentsInfo table. Two inventory configured Model Context Protocol servers, hunting anomalous endpoints and matching hostnames against ThreatIntelIndicators. The third lists active risk indicators per registered agent and resolves owner UPNs. If agents in your environment can reach arbitrary MCP endpoints, that configuration is now an evidence source.
- Sigma tuning matters if you run these rules. Five rules were updated, mostly to cut noise from Windows container activity (containerworker.exe). UAC bypass and shell open registry rules (ms-settings, exefile, sdclt.exe) gained exclusions for default IsolatedCommand and exefile values. The offline hive dump rule for reg.exe now requires SAM, SYSTEM, or SECURITY to directly follow the HKLM root key, so System32 and SystemTemp paths stop matching. The AMSI COM hijack rule (InProcServer32) now excludes valid amsi.dll paths across SysWOW64 and several environment variable notations. RDP Sensitive Settings Changed got stricter endswith matching on ServiceDll and exclusions for default termsrv.dll paths. If you forked these rules, diff them against upstream.
- Payload and email coverage. CAPEv2 updated YARA for BumbleBee Loader (BumbleBeeLoader and BumbleBeeShellcode), matching bytecode routines for API hooking, memory allocation, and section creation plus internal job strings. The shellcode rule filters out CAPE sandbox artifact strings. Sublime added 22 rules and updated 17. They cover PDF lures judged by EXIF producer metadata, OCR and YARA (fake remittance, Adobe-themed encrypted, SSA impersonation), AWS S3 website and image map credential theft, SiteScout /iap/ open redirects, and share[.]google redirect forms. Header rules catch randomized Mailer-[a-z0-9]{6,12} strings and malformed Outlook mailer strings. The OAuth consent rules now decode base64 query parameters. The sender indicator list was refreshed with new SHA-256 hashes.
Takeaway: if you collect process creation telemetry, test the new BITS upload logic against your own bitsadmin and Start-BitsTransfer history, and look for upload flags paired with non-corporate destinations. For the React rule, pivot from any Node.js child interpreter to its first public connection. The full rule names and source repos are listed in the report. Check them against your deployed versions before the next hunt cycle.

item.title: Rapid7 Detected Exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center, N-able N-central also Exploited
item.description:
Actively exploited: CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS 9.8), an unauthenticated RCE in end-of-life Apache Axis 1.x, is being used against Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central. Rapid7 MDR saw it against Confluence in a customer environment on November 13, 2026.
- The flaw is unsafe reflection (CWE-470) in Axis 1.x, a SOAP implementation for Java web services, disclosed by the Apache Software Foundation on November 6. Axis 1.x through 1.4 is EOL and Apache does not plan a fixed 1.x release. It recommends moving to another SOAP engine such as Axis 2, or using an Axis 1.x build with the published patch. Downstream products that bundle the library inherit the bug.
- Confluence Data Center: Atlassian lists 1.x through 9.x as affected only when "Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)" is enabled, which has been off by default for new installs since 3.0. 9.2.28 is the fixed release. 10.x removed the feature and Atlassian Cloud is unaffected. If you cannot patch yet, an admin can clear the setting under General Configuration > Further Configuration with no restart, but API integrations may break.
- N-able N-central: N-able reported in-the-wild exploitation on November 13 of a vulnerability that strongly correlates to CVE-2026-90436. A public PoC targeting N-central appeared on November 12 as part of a series of zero-day disclosures against the product. The exposure is the Legacy API, off by default, and admins should confirm it is disabled even on 2026.4 HF2. HF3 removes Legacy API access permanently. Hosted upgrades are done, on-prem GA is being finalized, and N-able temporarily disabled the Intune integration. Both hosting models still need to follow the Agent and Probe upgrade guidance.
- Timeline matters for scoping: disclosure November 6, PoC November 12, exploitation observed November 13. Any exposed instance with the relevant API enabled during that window is a candidate for compromise, and internal deployments count too.
- IOCs from the report. Confluence exploitation: 192.238.253[.]176, 5.133.47[.]243, 163.182.68[.]109, 104.13.106[.]166. N-able's November 13 incident update lists these for N-central customers who had not disabled Legacy API: 157.20.241[.]16, 139.99.69[.]109, 79.76.51[.]56. The vendor's update also lists associated URLs for compromise assessment.
Takeaway: patching or disabling the API closes the door but does not tell you whether someone already walked through. Check whether Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) on Confluence or Legacy API on N-central was enabled on each instance, then search your logs back to at least November 6 for the IPs above. A hit means start an investigation. A miss proves nothing, since Rapid7 notes that absence of these addresses does not confirm a clean environment. Preserve logs and host evidence before you change settings or upgrade. Since this is RCE, review the application hosts themselves for unexpected child processes, new files, and new accounts. N-central deserves extra attention because it manages downstream endpoints. The report has the Confluence IPs, and N-able's incident update has the N-central IOCs and URLs. Rapid7 recommends emergency remediation outside normal patch cycles.

item.title: Check Point Gateway Vulnerabilities Chained in Destructive Attacks
item.description:
Check Point Security Gateways are being chained from unauthenticated PHP2Shell remote code execution to root, then used to reach VMware ESXi and deploy the destroy_v6 wiper. Exploitation began October 30 against Israeli 🇮🇱 organizations and widened on November 2.
Check Point disclosed the active exploitation on November 12 after investigating multiple intrusions. The gateway was the platform, not the goal: the actors moved from the perimeter into virtualization infrastructure.
- Initial access: PHP2Shell is the name for two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS v4.0 9.2. They let a remote unauthenticated attacker run code through an exposed web interface, including the Mobile Access Portal. Affected are Security Gateways on R80 through R82.20 and Spark Firewall R81.10.x, R82.00.x, R77.20.x and R80.20.x with vulnerable web-facing services enabled. Exposure also covers Remote Access VPN with SNX or SAML, Identity Awareness Captive Portal, UserCheck Portal, and Zero Phishing.
- Root: PHP2Shell only gives execution in the portal service context. Attackers then used CVE-2026-123039 (CVSS v3.1 7.8), a local privilege escalation in the DynamicCLI service of Gaia OS, to reach root. It affects Gaia R81.20, R82, R82.10 and R82.20.
- Post-exploitation: actors dropped PHP web shells, installed the TSGA backdoor and TSProxy component for persistence, ran internal reconnaissance, and moved laterally. In the intrusion Check Point detailed, they reached an ESXi environment and deployed the destroy_v6 wiper on a host. Destructive activity hit a limited number of first-wave victims.
- Attribution is open. TSGA and TSProxy resemble the PhiliKit framework previously linked to UNC5221, but Check Point says the evidence does not support high-confidence attribution. It floated several scenarios: a full operation by one actor, an initial access broker, a false flag, or destruction as a smoke screen.
- Gateway artifacts to check: PHP session files containing upload_progress_pwn, unexpected template files such as zz*.tpl and challenge_render.tpl, TSGA and TSProxy artifacts, unexpected CPconfigdaemon processes, /lib/libcpfwcommon.so, listeners on TCP port 11072, anomalous outbound connections, and gaps in logging.
Timeline matters here. PHP fixed the flaws October 21 and Check Point shipped a standalone gateway hotfix October 23, so the first wave on October 30 came after fixes existed. The Gaia privilege escalation fix arrived in the November 12 Jumbo Hotfix. Patching closes the path but does not remove access gained earlier.
Takeaway: if a gateway ran an exposed vulnerable service at any point since October 30, treat it as a compromise assessment, not a patch ticket. Sweep it for the artifacts above, then pivot downstream. On ESXi hosts and other reachable systems, look for SSH activity originating from gateway addresses, use of the vpxuser account on ESXi, unexpected administrative actions, and signs of destructive activity. Extend the review to vCenter, management networks, identity services, and backup systems reachable from the gateway. Preserve gateway logs first, since log gaps are themselves an indicator.
Minimum fixed Jumbo Hotfix releases are R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, and R81.20 Take 174. R81.10 and older need an upgrade to a supported release. IPS protections CPAI-2026-15172 and CPAI-2026-15184 cover PHP2Shell as a stopgap. The report lists artifact types, not a hash or IP IOC list.

item.title: Europe's fridge attacks, up close: 110 °C typed into Copeland XWEB from an iPhone
item.description:
Factory-default Admin / Admin let one person on an iPhone rewrite two Copeland XWEB refrigeration decoys: set point 110 °C, alarms maxed, keypads locked. No exploit was needed.
- The researchers' decoys saw the login on 13 Nov. Admin / Admin was accepted first try on both units. In about an hour, from 169.150.218[.]23, the visitor made 39 parameter writes and 103 commands across the twelve Dixell controllers each unit supervises. The block pushed fields to their maximums: SEt 110, LS 110, US 🇺🇸 150, ALU and ALL 255, ALd 255, dAO 23, dtE and dtS 50, MdF 255. Then, controller by controller: Light OFF, Alarm Mute, KeyboardLock. The case looks off, stays silent, and can't be fixed from its front panel. It matches the French 🇫🇷 incidents, where units reportedly ran at 50 °C for six hours with lengthened defrosts delaying alarms.
- This was typed by hand. Every request carried Chrome 157 on iOS 26.6.2. Six writes contain 11” where 110 was meant (a phone keyboard's closing quote), two controllers got 155 instead of 255, and the visitor later unlocked, retyped and relocked two of the mistyped controllers. Both session tokens were then replayed from 169.224.124[.]75 (Earthlink, Iraq), 84.252.113[.]54, 84.252.113[.]57 (Datacamp, France 🇫🇷) and 80.79.6[.]92 (WorldStream, Netherlands 🇳🇱). All writes came from the first address; the rest only refreshed device lists, the pattern of a VPN dropping and reconnecting.
- The same phone came back. On 14 Nov 12:00 it logged in again from 80.79.6[.]92 and only watched. On 15 Nov 22:37, from 185.107.80[.]116, it opened a third decoy with Admin / Admin, then hand-typed admin; sleep 5 # with password jakakak. That tests CVE-2026-124002, the XWEB EVO pre-auth username command injection that runs as root. It then tried Administrator with xwebevonewgeneration, the hard-coded password in CVE-2026-124004. Both records were published 12 Nov.
- Scripts were faster. The first scripted request hit a decoy at 21:44 UTC on 12 Nov from 202.61.138[.]117, under two hours after publication: POST /cgi-bin/sysinfo.lua, POST /cgi-bin/config.lua, GET /cgi-bin/xwconsole.cgi (CVE-2026-124011, CVE-2026-124014, CVE-2026-124010). Others followed: xwconsole.cgi?sh=id from 154.9.235[.]100, a marker echo from 177.4.12[.]11, and a paced scanner posting username=user$(sleep 8) to /login.lua, /cleanout.lua and /api.lua.
Takeaway: audit parameters against your commissioning sheet. On each controller check SEt, LS, US 🇺🇸, ALU, ALL, ALd, dAO, dtE and MdF. Values at the top of range (110, 150, 255, 50, 23) are what this session left behind. A dark case with a locked keypad and no alarm is the visible sign. In web logs, hunt for logins from addresses that aren't your maintenance provider, usernames containing ;, $( or a backtick, an Administrator login you didn't make, and any request to xwconsole.cgi. Change every default password and take the interface off the internet. The CVE records say XWEB EVO is end of service since March 2026, with the hard-coded password in versions before 5.6.2 and the injection before 5.7.0. The full IOC table is in the report.

item.title: Turla Serves Up Cereal Malware to Spy on Governments
item.description:
Russia-aligned Turla is running an eight-component toolset, dubbed Cereal by ESET, against government organizations in Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 and Romania 🇷🇴 since late 2025. It turns compromised Exchange servers into passive C2 endpoints and in-memory email collectors.
- Passive C2 on the mail server itself: CerealNeuron uses the HttpListener class to watch predefined URL prefixes on the compromised Exchange server. Operators send RSA-2048 and AES encrypted requests carrying .NET assemblies, usually wrapped by CerealRunner. Invalid requests can be redirected to Exchange error pages. Observed paths: /owa/sdds/, /autodiscover/microsoft.exchange.proxyservice/, /autodiscover/integrated/api/, /autodiscover/proxyservice/, /microsoft-server-activesync/integrated/api/. ESET saw no dedicated external C2 and could not identify the source IPs, so there may be no beaconing to find. CerealHermit is the file-based sibling that reads encrypted commands from disk, and several victims had both deployed.
- Mail interception in the transport pipeline: CerealBox arrives through a chain of CerealRunner, CerealMoth, CerealIron and CerealSprinter. It was likely injected into EdgeTransport.exe, though operators supplied the process ID, so ESET could not confirm the target. It does not register a new transport agent. It replaces existing routing agent factories in memory with wrappers that preserve the original behavior, so mail flow looks normal. ESET calls this a previously undocumented technique. It selects messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match sender, recipient, subject or filename criteria. In the Romanian 🇷🇴 case the filters covered nato[.]int and europa[.]eu addresses. Matches are serialized, compressed, encrypted and staged to disk, with a new file once data passes 5 MB. It stops 70 days after first execution.
- Loading and stealth tradecraft: CerealLoader uses a native entry point and .NET VTable Fixups to run managed code in processes that would not normally start the .NET runtime. ESET saw DLL search order hijacking where a malicious wbemcomn.dll in the WMI directory was loaded by the legitimate WmiPrvSE.exe, forwarding genuine calls to keep things working. Other variants planted files in the .NET native image cache under names resembling Exchange assemblies, so the runtime executes them on load. - Post-exploitation scope: ESET observed thousands of CerealRunner binaries with commands for mailbox retrieval, Active Directory enumeration, WMI queries, file operations and LSA secrets extraction. Initial access is undetermined, though exploitation of internet-facing Exchange vulnerabilities is considered possible.
- Lineage: Turla (Snake, Venomous Bear, Waterbug, Secret Blizzard, Uroboros) is widely assessed to be tied to Russia's 🇷🇺 FSB and has been active since at least 2004. This continues the LightNeuron playbook of using Exchange as the control channel. ESET also documented Turla's Kazuar backdoor being deployed through Gamaredon tooling in 2025.

Check for wbemcomn.dll in the WMI directory that is not the genuine library, and for files in the .NET native image cache that imitate Exchange assemblies. Inspect EdgeTransport.exe for injected code and unexpected assemblies loaded in memory. Look for encrypted staging files on disk, since that is where collected mail lands. Capture memory before rebooting, because most components never touch disk unencrypted. CerealLoader SHA-256 hashes are listed in the report.

item.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
item.description:
GTIG and Mandiant report that adversaries now run open source multi-agent offensive frameworks in live intrusions and have fully automated patch diffing to exploit n-days with no human in the loop. Meanwhile LLMJacking has pushed single-day fraud past $100,000 in IR cases.
- Agentic intrusion tooling is in the wild. GTIG saw CAIRN used against targets including the aerospace sector in the US 🇺🇸, and a customized PentAGI-based platform used from late August to early October 2026 for recon and vulnerability scanning of organizations in Asia. CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, ZeroHollow and Agent Zero were seen in experimentation, and a PRC-nexus group was building its own framework. The report says these tools trade stealth for velocity: they generate forensic traffic, use recognizable identifiers and leave code-level traces.
- Patch-to-exploit is collapsing. GTIG found an exposed staging server running exploit_agent, which diffs web app code before and after patches, drafts exploits and fires them automatically. Post-compromise scripts covered internal recon, brute-forcing, webshell install and removal of other attackers' webshells. Victim data pointed to French 🇫🇷 media, entertainment and education sites, and the env file had Russian-language comments. Related: PaperCut CVE-2026-81578 (auth bypass) chained with CVE-2026-82078 (unsafe dynamic class loading) gave unauthenticated RCE as zero-days. Greynoise reported a likely LLM-built campaign four days after disclosure that reached domain admin within minutes. Zero-day exploits rose from 8 per month in 2025 to 11 in 2026, then hit 22 in August.
- LLMJacking is a cloud IR problem. Mandiant saw stolen credentials and session tokens (including keys harvested from public GitHub repos) used to enable LLM services, subscribe accounts to pay-as-you-go, provision GPU instances and request quota increases. Persistence was privileged service accounts and admin policies attached to service roles, no malware needed. One actor used "burn and rotate" short-lived service accounts. One actor exploited CVE-2026-40217, a LiteLLM sandbox escape that turns limited Virtual Keys into admin credentials. Costs reached $100,000+ in a day and $1 million cumulative. In one case a botnet or proxy pool sharing a User-Agent made millions of API calls in about 24 hours on the same credentials as another actor. Access is resold through LLM Mixers at $0.10 to $25 per million tokens.
- AI tooling is now a supply chain and C2 surface. Suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE (DPRK activity) hit crypto firms in North America and Europe with fake recruiter profiles, ClickFix lures, then edited .claude/settings.json in internal repos so Claude Code startup downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor. It also minted GitHub PATs named after Microsoft Copilot to blend in. Separately, PRC-nexus actors abused LLM platforms and file-hosting backends for staging, dead-drop C2 and exfiltration; one used a frontier model's file hosting to stage lures and exfiltrate data. Iranian 🇮🇷 CALANQUE ION (formerly APT42) keeps using LLMs for recon and social engineering. PRC contractor LEAKY CASTLE used LLMs to analyze and translate exfiltrated data.
- IO and crime scale up too. An IaaS platform used residential proxies and saved login cookies to dodge CAPTCHAs, and another was built to manage over 100,000 accounts via cloud phone farms. The Jieyou PhaaS added an LLM chatbot to its backend in June 2026 to configure phishing panels in natural language.
Takeaway: treat AI developer tooling and cloud AI quotas as in-scope evidence. Diff .claude/settings.json and agent config files in internal repos for new hook or download entries. Audit PATs for lookalike names such as Copilot. In cloud, review IAM changes for service accounts created and deleted in short order, admin policy attachments to service roles, GPU instance launches, quota increase requests and new pay-as-you-go subscriptions, and correlate with billing spikes and shared User-Agents. Expect noisy automation to leave scan traffic and recognizable identifiers, so preserve web and cloud logs from the first hours of any n-day window.

item.title: Twelve Minutes in ScreenConnect's Backstage
item.description:
A fake Adobe update installed ScreenConnect, and twelve hours later an operator spent twelve minutes in hidden Backstage mode as SYSTEM. Script block logging was off, so the session had to be rebuilt from artifacts.
- Lure and install: an email in personal webmail opened on a work laptop led to hxxps://151uneven.northbox[.]us/622liberalism/ ("PDF Viewer"), then hxxps://sipberco[.]es/Installer/Adobe.html. That page served a ScreenConnect cloud installer built from ScreenConnect's own query string (e=Access, y=Guest, c=Acrobat). The user accepted the admin prompt and ran it four times. It installed under C:\Program Files (x86)\ScreenConnect Client (<instance-id>)\ as a SYSTEM auto-start service and added its DLL to HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Authentication Packages. Two seconds after the service started it was talking to instance-yq5koz-relay.screenconnect[.]com.
- The operator session (T1219.002): at 12:58:34 UTC a 745-character command ran through ScreenConnect's command feature as SYSTEM. It added a Defender exclusion for C:\Users and used powercfg to disable sleep, hibernation and the lid-close action. Backstage connected at 12:59:00 and a second installer was pushed over file transfer at 12:59:06. That second client pointed at an attacker-run relay on TCP 8041 (relay.gronadfrostvault[.]site, 178.173.246[.]29) as a backup door. The EDR killed it four seconds after launch, and again on the retry at 13:04:20. The service, authentication package and a credential provider (ScreenConnect.WindowsCredentialProvider.dll) stayed on disk. The operator left at 13:11:00.
- HideUL (T1564): the operator pulled Backup[.]zip into C:\Users three times. It held Sordum's Hide From Uninstall List, meant to hide the rogue clients from Programs and Features. The $MFT, USN journal and Recycle Bin show HideUL.exe deleted about a second after each unzip. There was no Prefetch, no Program Compatibility Assistant record and no process event, so it never ran. SHA-256 4967e47b19d372bb7337f0c4dcd586da88dd01e8b64d63ff86e0f78bf4981c85. The same playbook appeared five months earlier at another customer, with HideUL_x64.exe and an HFULOption value under the uninstall keys.
- Scoping with no typed-command logs: the consoles ran as SYSTEM, so PSReadLine history sat under C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt and held one line. ScreenConnect's Application log gave event 20 (relay connect), 100/101 (operator connect and disconnect with display name), 200 (command, length only) and 201 (file transfer, action Run). SRUM showed the client service sent 816,121 B that hour, session traffic included, which rules out a bulk grab but not a few small files. The SYSTEM account's hive at C:\Windows\System32\config\DEFAULT showed a file picker opened at 13:10:55 with nothing selected. OneDrive logs explained odd folder access times as a registry-triggered refresh. Sysmon showed no ScreenConnect, PowerShell or cmd process opening LSASS, and Credential Guard was running.
- The gap: a SYSTEM PowerShell console can read and decrypt Chrome's Login Data, and nothing on that laptop would log it. If an operator had SYSTEM and you cannot rule that out, treat every password saved in the browser as exposed and rotate it.
Takeaway: when an operator worked in Backstage, collect the SYSTEM profile's PSReadLine history, the DEFAULT hive and the ScreenConnect Application events along with the user's artifacts. Hunt ScreenConnect.WindowsBackstageShell.exe as a parent of cmd or PowerShell, and ScreenConnect sessions installing another remote access client. Reimage rather than uninstall, since each client registered its own LSA package and the second added a credential provider. Turn on script block logging on workstations. Sigma rules (Backstage shell, MSI pushed over RunFile, powercfg from a ScreenConnect script, HideUL file and process, hidden uninstall entries) and the IOC table are in the report.

item.title: Fake Prime Gaming x FC 27 reward site harvests EA passwords and 2FA codes
item.description:
A fake "FC27 x Prime Gaming" reward site is phishing EA SPORTS FC 27 players. It clones the EA sign-in, captures email, password and the six-digit 2FA code in real time, then bounces victims to the real ea[.]com so nothing looks wrong.
Malwarebytes Labs found the lure after the game's September 25 launch. It promises a waiting Prime Gaming reward and asks the visitor to "connect" an EA account. There is no reward. The sign-in that follows is a copy hosted on the scammers' own domain.
- Lure and flow: the landing page says "Connecting..." and "Redirecting to EA authorization...", waits a fixed 1.4 seconds, then moves the victim to /in on the same domain. The cloned login has a "Phone or Email" field, "Keep me signed in," a passkey option and Google, Facebook, Apple and Steam buttons. The social buttons do nothing and only steer the victim toward typing credentials.
- Exfiltration: each step posts to a separate server, fedserv.thenewsip[.]site. Email goes first, then the password. The page uses the server's reply to decide whether to show an EA-style "Your credentials are incorrect" error or move on to a "Verify your identity" page that asks for the six-digit code. Malwarebytes says this is consistent with an attempt to check the details against EA, but the captured page code alone doesn't confirm how the server handles the data. Accounts without 2FA skip the code step. The victim is then redirected to EA's real Ultimate Team web app.
- Why 2FA doesn't save you here: a captured code isn't a bypass of 2FA itself, but it could let the attacker finish a sign-in before the code expires. Landing on the real ea[.]com at the end doesn't mean the earlier sign-in was legitimate.
- Traffic tracking: the page logs the visitor's source and sends it with the stolen data. It recognizes Facebook, Messenger, Meta's Audience Network, Instagram and TikTok through tracking parameters and the fbclid and ttclid click IDs. Everything else is labeled "direct" or "unknown." The kit also supports Umami analytics, though the settings file wasn't captured. This shows the page was built to handle social-platform traffic, not that ads actually ran there.
- Evasion and configuration: the HTML asks search engines not to index, archive or preview it and calls itself a private team tool. The Privacy Policy and Terms pages describe an internal authentication portal for authorized personnel. Two switches exist: one disables the Prime Gaming lure so the kit shows a plain fake EA login, the other chooses between redirecting to real EA or showing an "enrolled for weekly FC 27 rewards" page. In the analyzed version, both the lure and the EA redirect were on.
- Impact: an EA account can hold an FC Ultimate Team club with coins and tradable players, purchased games and saved payment methods. A hijacked account can also be used to message the victim's gaming contacts with scam links.
Domain IOCs are listed in the report: fc27-prime[.]shop, fc27prime[.]shop, fc27utprime[.]com, fc27utprime[.]online, fcutprime[.]online, plus the collection host fedserv.thenewsip[.]site.
Practitioner takeaway: for anyone who may have entered details, the evidence is on the account side. Check DNS and proxy logs for any of these domains, especially fedserv.thenewsip[.]site, to scope exposure. A hit on fedserv.thenewsip[.]site indicates submitted data, so treat the credentials and any 2FA code as stolen, even if the browser ended on ea[.]com; a lure-domain hit alone shows a visit. Then change the EA password from ea[.]com directly, remove unfamiliar trusted devices, and review changes to the email address, linked accounts and purchases. Reset any reused passwords, starting with the email account.

item.title: Typosquatters Copy Big Brands’ New Domains Within a Day of Registration
item.description:
Typosquatters registered one-letter lookalikes, like carmaxclaim[.]com, within a day of CSC and MarkMonitor brand registrations. Check RDAP for one-letter variants of new domains; IOCs are in Symantec's report.

item.title: SANSAR Linux Cryptomining Malware Uses Modified NVIDIA Library to Hide GPU Activity
item.description:
REF3364 is running a Linux cryptomining operation that lies to GPU monitoring. Its SANSAR toolkit pairs a ftrace rootkit with a modified NVML wrapper so nvidia-smi shows 0% utilization while miners run. Elastic Security Labs observed it in late October 2026.
- Entry and persistence: initial access came through an exposed Ray job agent. The actor ran jobs that executed nvidia-smi and sent the GPU inventory to an external server, then submitted a Python reverse shell job to a remote listener. An SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys for persistent access. After obtaining root, the toolkit was staged under /opt/vadi_.
- Rootkit and boot persistence: the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module was built through DKMS, and an initramfs loader was added. Because the module and loader sit in the boot image on disk, the rootkit loads again whenever the host boots with that image. It uses ftrace to intercept system calls for directory listings, file access, and process termination signals. It strips matching process, file, and socket entries and returns "No such file or directory" or "No such process" for hidden items.
- Telemetry falsification: the modified NVML wrapper hooks calls used by tools like nvidia-smi. It reports GPU utilization as 0%, and replaces temperature and power with random values between 36 and 46 degrees Celsius and 100 to 200 watts. It also filters process information.
- Payloads: sansar is a Rust orchestrator that talks to an onion C2 via Arti (efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion). It starts and stops miners, updates configs, spawns interactive shells, launches an IPv4 TCP SYN traffic task against a given address and port, and maintains the NVML hook. It reads TracerPid first and exits if a tracer is attached. Its CPU branch launches kurt (XMRig 6.25.0) and its GPU branch launches tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI 3.6.9). lyrebird is a legitimate Tor pluggable transport proxy.
- Second backdoor: netns runs as a systemd service. It queries an embedded Ethereum smart contract (0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349) for a controller IPv4 address, then opens a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080 and starts a reverse shell to the host and port in the response. Attribution is unclear, but the rootkit source contains Turkish 🇹🇷 language comments.
Why it matters: GPU hosts for AI and LLM workloads are expensive, and a tampered NVML makes the usual "is the GPU busy" check worthless. Cryptojacking diverts compute and raises costs.
Takeaway: do not trust on-host tooling on a suspect GPU node. Image the disk and inspect from outside the running system: the initramfs, the DKMS build for acpi_thermal_mgr, /opt/vadi_, authorized_keys, and systemd units for netns. Verify the NVML library has not been modified, and review who can submit jobs to Ray and whether the job agent is exposed. Also check for anomalies like a "0%" GPU on a node with high out-of-band (BMC/PDU) power or heat, since NVML temperature and power are faked too, and hunt at the network level for outbound Tor (incl. lyrebird bridges) and port 8080 connections from GPU hosts.

item.title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys
item.description:
AI agents likely built on the ARTEX pentest tool are hunting exposed LiteLLM, Dify and One API apps for stored AI provider keys, per Amazon's decoy records. Cloudflare saw ARTEX in real incidents too.
- Amazon's MadPot decoys, posing as LLM services, received agent requests from October 3 that often carried full campaign history: operator instructions and the agents' findings. Amazon assesses with moderate confidence that the operators are separate China-linked groups (Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 prompts, China 🇨🇳 time zone settings). It did not see the activity on victim systems and cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported. Records cover hundreds of targets, and AWS customers who may have been affected were notified.
- The playbook lists entry points per product. Targets: One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM, Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat and Ollama. Entries include default admin credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs an outsider can claim, unauthenticated management and provider settings endpoints, an isCliRequest header auth bypass in One API family systems, and SSRF through URL-fetch features to reach cloud metadata services. Also covered: secrets in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes and environment files. Keys get verified and added to a shared pool. Leaked-key hunting spans internet scanning services, certificate transparency logs, GitHub, npm and PyPI, container image layers, notebooks, paste sites and Telegram.
- Named flaws: Langflow CVE-2025-3248 is missing authentication enabling remote code execution. Versions before 1.3.0 are affected, 1.3.0 fixes it, and it has been in CISA KEV since May 5, 2025, marked as used in ransomware campaigns. RAGFlow CVE-2026-28797 is SSTI letting any logged-in user run OS commands. Self-registration is on by default, NVD lists 0.24.0 and earlier, the advisory lists no patched version, and 0.25.0 renders templates in the recommended sandbox. The report names no versions or fix for the One API bypass.
- Cloudflare's responders saw ARTEX use an account-level API token from CI/CD with no IP restrictions or rate limiting. Activity included 400 database dump requests in an hour (whether data came back is undisclosed) and more than 69 requests per minute across the account. It also included persistence attempts and session token validation for other third-party apps. New Worker scripts appeared named artex-*, artex-pgrecon-*, artex-pgw-* and artex-do-*. The common root cause across incidents was static, never-expiring CI/CD tokens. The initial token theft has not been disclosed.
- Scale: the FBI FLASH alert says ARTEX has been used since at least August, summarizing 11 earlier reports. The repo went down October 8, but forks, archives and ARTEX PRO remain. Cloudflare saw more than 50 AI pentest framework families scan its customers in three days.
Takeaway: treat any AI gateway as a credential vault. Hunt Cloudflare accounts for Worker scripts matching the artex-* names and review account-level tokens lacking expiry or IP limits. Rotate any provider key stored in an exposed gateway, and check provider-side usage and spend for unexpected activity. Check logs for the 11 IPs published with Amazon's decoy findings and Cisco Talos's indicator files (2,500+ IPs). Talos Snort rules: Snort 3 7:76, 7:77, 7:78 and Snort 2 1:67494, 1:67495, 1:67496. Rules 7:78 and 1:67496 are off by default and detect traces of norma, the harness ARTEX uses.

item.title: A USB worm’s second life: Retadup spreading CoffeeLoader
item.description:
Retadup, the USB worm French 🇫🇷 police wiped from 850,000 machines in 2019, is back as a CoffeeLoader delivery channel. Re-registered Retadup C2 domains now push a new Armoury-packed CoffeeLoader variant that Kaspersky spotted in August 2026.
- Chain: an NSIS installer drops 7z.dll, a patched 7-Zip library whose code was replaced with self-decrypting shellcode, and runs it through rundll32.exe. The shellcode is a new Armoury packer that decrypts on the GPU via an OpenGL compute shader XOR, where the old one used OpenCL. It then delivers a new intermediate CoffeeLoader downloader that carries the dropper and stager logic plus the download function.
- Persistence artifacts: 7z.dll is copied to a subfolder of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%, with folder, DLL, and Run value named from eight hex digits derived from system volume information. Example: C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll, launched by the Run key as rundll32.exe with export SetCodecs. It also writes a StartupApproved\Run value of 080000000000000000000000 so the user cannot disable autorun in Task Manager.
- Download and C2: the downloader launches one of dllhost.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe, OpenWith.exe, or AtBroker.exe and injects itself into it. It then pulls the main body over HTTPS from api.internet-speed-check[.]com using GET /payload?md5=, with zeros on the first request and the previous payload hash afterward. The request uses a Firefox 152.0 user agent and the server sits behind Cloudflare. The response is XOR-encrypted with its first 16 bytes as key. X-Signature is checked against an embedded public key and X-Content-MD5 against the decrypted body before control moves to executable memory.
- Main module: functionally unchanged. It has new C2 encryption keys (A21251838432306F2CD2540593656B9E and 2026F751079659CF71C7BA64B345C12A), and signature checks replace certificate validation. The magic constant 0xC0FFEE42 is now 0xD1D57871. It keeps the same three commands: inject a payload, save it as an EXE and run it, or save it as a DLL and run it via rundll32.exe.
- Retadup revival: this AutoIt/AutoHotkey worm spreads through hidden files and LNK shortcuts on USB and external drives. Someone began re-registering its C2 domains in 2024, first serving SmokeLoader and then CoffeeLoader in early 2025. The protocol is just Base64 converted to hex, so anyone could revive it. A 2017 variant still gets commands in 2026, such as a download-hxxp://rurjfvn[.]rs/update.exe instruction. Kaspersky blocked Retadup infection attempts on about 15,000 systems, mostly in Peru 🇵🇪, Angola, Russia 🇷🇺, and Bolivia.
Takeaway: hunt for rundll32.exe loading a DLL with export SetCodecs from an eight-hex-digit folder under %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%. Check Run key values pointing at it and a matching StartupApproved\Run entry. A 7z.dll outside a real 7-Zip install is a red flag. On the network, look for GET /payload?md5=00000000000000000000000000000000 and DNS to the Retadup domains, such as alphanoob[.]com and newblackage[.]com. Image USB media for hidden files and LNK shortcuts to find patient zero, and inspect memory of the injected system processes. The report lists the Retadup and CoffeeLoader C2s, the hosting URLs, and MD5s for the DLLs and NSIS installers.

item.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
item.description:
BO Team exploited Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) on VMware vCenter 7.0.3 to reach a Russian 🇷🇺 developer's CI/CD and code-signing server, per Kaspersky. Backdoors, LotL tooling and log deletion hid a likely supply chain play.
- Entry and pivot: BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, Lifting Zmiy), assessed to be of Ukrainian 🇺🇦 origin, got in through an exposed SSH service on a Linux terminal server and scanned internal SMB, Kerberos, SSH, WinRM, LDAP and more. Direct vCenter logins failed, but the unpatched vCenter 7.0.3 fell to Log4Shell, giving a root command line and SSH access to the hypervisor. Kaspersky ICS CERT was called in June 2025.
- Hypervisor persistence: a shell script named pgcache, dressed up as a PostgreSQL component, was dropped in /etc/cron.hourly/ and runs every hour. It pulls a second script from lo1yaizaeghaevarooD1ahtaichootae.nofrillsdns[.]com, which fetches the GSocket utility for remote control. Some variants point to lo1yaizaeghaevarood1ahtaichootaz.nofrillsdns[.]com for a hostname-specific payload. The operators keep the DNS record at 127.0.0.1 while idle and flip it to activate the backdoor. The hypervisor's certificate was then abused to plant a similar backdoor on a second virtualization cluster.
- Credential and lateral movement: secrets found on VMs led to the GitLab VM, some of its source repositories and its private key, which opened the Ansible orchestration system. On Windows, they dumped lsass.exe through comsvcs.dll after Nanodump was blocked, dumped the registry with regedit.exe to decrypt ntds.dit, and moved data to the terminal server with scp.exe. Reused admin passwords across domains and a Kerberos ticket gave full domain control. They also modified /usr/bin/nxnode-login to write captured credentials to /dev/shm/pulse-shm-3088612174, and brute-forced the terminal server admin password after about 2,500 failed attempts.
- Anti-forensics: timestomping, obfuscated bash that decrypts and runs an ELF SSH remote-control binary, systematic event log deletion, malware named like legitimate software, and heavy use of RDP, SSH, SCP, tasklist.exe, findstr.exe and ipconfig.exe. The attackers also changed security attributes on a user's Windows Downloads directory.
- Why it matters: of the Windows servers they touched, malware was used on only one, the server that signs builds of the victim's commercial software. A WMI script and a backdoor in the temp directory were likely attempted there. Kaspersky sees either build tampering before signing or theft of the signing identity. No destruction or public claim followed. After losing access, the actors sent a late-July phishing mail ("Account disconnected from the mail server") that passed SPF and DKIM, suggesting a stolen mail server private key. Activity came from 193.3.23[.]236 and 80.76.42[.]139, both at a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 provider.
Takeaway: treat the hypervisor as a crime scene, not just the guests. Check cron.hourly for pgcache, look for DNS lookups of nofrillsdns[.]com (including 127.0.0.1 answers), inspect nxnode-login and /dev/shm for the credential file, and review comsvcs.dll lsass access and registry dumps on Windows. If a build or signing host was reachable, audit recent signed builds and consider the signing key exposed. Since logs were wiped, rely on off-host copies. The report lists the domains and IPs above.
